title: Boring-NixOS
text:
Boring NixOS
A direct, practical guide to configuring infrastructure that builds identically every time: deterministic, immutable, and refreshingly boring.
Ambiguity is the enemy of reliability. When machines mutate silently through ad-hoc commands, builds drift, onboarding breaks, and outages follow. The boring default is to define the full closure in code — from developer compilers to multi-region cloud clusters — so every environment evaluates identically six months later.
Baseline: Nix 2.24+ · NixOS 24.11+ · Flakes enabled. Standalone and self-contained. You do not need any other title in this library.

title: Boring-NixOS
text:
Who this is for

Engineers, platform developers, and SREs who want systems that build identically on a laptop, CI runner, and bare-metal server.
Developers looking for instant, clean project environments without container lag or host library pollution.
Teams moving away from fragile setup scripts and mutable system administration toward pure declarative configuration.

You do not need prior experience with Nix or functional programming. A terminal, a standard text editor, and basic Linux familiarity are all you need.

title: Boring-NixOS
text:
What “boring” means here
Nix is a purely functional package manager and domain-specific language. Applied with discipline, it eliminates entire categories of operational bugs: conflicting shared libraries, broken symlinks, broken OS upgrades, and undocumented host drift.
When over-complicated, it can become an impenetrable maze of nested overlays and tangled macros.
Boring NixOS teaches clear, sustainable defaults: - Plain, readable expressions over clever meta-programming. - Explicit inputs pinned by cryptographic lockfiles. - Modular, auditable NixOS system definitions that scale without surprise.

title: Boring-NixOS
text:
How to read

Read the chapter concept and mental model.
Type the expression into its designated file (default.nix, shell.nix, flake.nix, or configuration.nix).
Run the exact build or evaluation command.
Experiment with the Try this exercises to verify how the store and evaluator behave.

The chapters are sequenced progressively. You can jump directly to devShells, NixOS services, or CI caching once you know the language basics.

title: Boring-NixOS
text:
How examples work
Every code listing is a complete, runnable expression or file. Nothing is an incomplete fragment left for you to guess.
# default.nix
let
  message = "reproducible desk online";
in
message
nix-instantiate --eval default.nix
"reproducible desk online"
A recurring scenario — a small team infrastructure desk (workstations, devShells, microservices, deployment pipelines) — connects the exercises so each technique solves a practical engineering challenge.

title: Boring-NixOS
text:
What this book is not

Not an exhaustive reference manual of all 100,000+ packages in nixpkgs.
Not an exercise in esoteric functional programming puzzles.
Not a guide to maintaining legacy channels and unpinned channels.

It is a concrete guide to writing reproducible systems that remain easy to understand, maintain, and operate.

title: The Reproducibility Crisis
text:
The Reproducibility Crisis
Software engineering has spent decades tolerating ambient state: hidden dependencies, global machine mutations, and “works on my machine” excuses. The boring default of this book is: every development environment, dependency, and production system must be a pure, declarative, reproducible expression from zero.

title: The Reproducibility Crisis
text:
Mental model
Traditional operations rely on imperative mutation. You provision a virtual machine or container, run a sequence of apt-get, curl | bash, and pip install commands, and hope that: 1. Upstream package repositories haven’t updated or removed files. 2. Network connections remain uninterrupted mid-install. 3. System state matches the exact sequence of commands previously tested.
When any of these fail, you get Heisenbugs: intermittent build failures, subtle ABI mismatches, and production outages that disappear when you attempt to isolate them.
Traditional Imperative Model:
  Base OS -> [Step 1: apt-get] -> [Step 2: pip install] -> [Step 3: git clone] -> ??? (Unknown state)

Nix Declarative Model:
  Inputs (Source + Hashes) -> Pure Derivation -> Immutable /nix/store Path (Deterministic)
Nix replaces stateful mutation with pure mathematical evaluation: given the exact same source code and inputs, it always yields the exact same byte-for-byte system closure.

title: The Reproducibility Crisis
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Detecting Ambient Host Contamination
Save as test_environment.sh. Inspect how standard shell scripts unknowingly depend on host binaries and paths.
# test_environment.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

echo "Inspecting system path dependencies:"
which python3 || echo "python3 missing"
which node || echo "node missing"
which gcc || echo "gcc missing"
Run:
bash test_environment.sh
Output (on a typical developer workstation):
Inspecting system path dependencies:
/usr/bin/python3
/home/user/.nvm/versions/node/v20.0.0/bin/node
/usr/bin/gcc
Notice how three completely different tools live in three different unpinned locations (/usr/bin, user home directories, global OS paths). If a colleague runs the exact same script on a fresh laptop, it fails immediately.


Case 2: Purity and Isolated Evaluation
Save as pure_check.nix. A minimal Nix expression evaluated in isolation.
# pure_check.nix
let
  system = builtins.currentSystem;
  message = "No ambient host contamination allowed";
in
{
  inherit system message;
}
Run:
nix-instantiate --eval pure_check.nix
Output:
{ message = "No ambient host contamination allowed"; system = "x86_64-linux"; }
Evaluating this expression does not query the internet, look at /usr/local, or depend on environment variables.


Case 3: Hermetic Sandboxing in Action
Nix builds run in sandboxed namespaces where network access and non-declared filesystem paths are inaccessible.
Save as sandbox_check.nix:
# sandbox_check.nix
derivation {
  name = "sandbox-proof";
  system = builtins.currentSystem;
  builder = "/bin/sh";
  args = [
    "-c"
    "echo 'Built inside isolated namespace' > $out"
  ];
}
Run:
nix-build sandbox_check.nix
Output:
these 1 derivations will be built:
  /nix/store/10h9v...-sandbox-proof.drv
building '/nix/store/10h9v...-sandbox-proof.drv'...
/nix/store/v73ka...-sandbox-proof
Inspect output:
cat result
Output:
Built inside isolated namespace
The output was generated purely from the declared inputs.

title: The Reproducibility Crisis
text:
The trap
Relying on “Golden Images” (pre-baked AMIs, Docker images without lockfiles, or manual server setup steps documented in internal wikis).
Wiki page: "Run these 14 commands to set up the desk service..."
By week three, one PPA repository goes offline, a patch release bumps a minor dependency, and onboarding is broken for every new hire.
The fix: Check in code that defines the environment completely down to cryptographic hashes. If it builds once, it builds forever.

title: The Reproducibility Crisis
text:
The boring rule

Never mutate system state in-place with ad-hoc shell commands.
Pin all toolchain and library dependencies via cryptographic hashes.
Eliminate dependency on the host’s ambient /usr/bin and $PATH.
Every environment must be reproducible from a fresh Git checkout.

title: The Reproducibility Crisis
text:
Try this

Run env in your current shell and note how many variables point to user home directories or mutable local paths.
In pure_check.nix, add a field timestamp = builtins.currentTime; and observe how pure evaluation restricts non-deterministic built-ins.

title: The /nix/store Anatomy
text:
The /nix/store Anatomy
The Nix store is the foundation of reproducible systems. Every entry follows a strict naming convention:
For example:

title: The /nix/store Anatomy
text:
Worked examples
Examine a store path directly in your shell.
Run:
ls -ld $(which nix)
Output:
-r-xr-xr-x 1 root root 15728640 Jan 1 1970 /nix/store/7vqw9388...-nix-2.24.1/bin/nix
Notice: - Permissions are -r-xr-xr-x (read and execute only; no write permission). - The timestamp is standardized to Jan 1 1970 (Unix epoch) to preserve bit-for-bit build reproducibility across time zones.

title: The /nix/store Anatomy
text:
The boring rule

All binaries and libraries live strictly under /nix/store.
Never manually move or rename files inside the store.

title: Content-Addressable Paths
text:
Content-Addressable Paths
Historically, Nix paths were input-addressed (the hash was computed from inputs). Content-addressable paths hash the final built artifact itself.

title: Content-Addressable Paths
text:
Mental model

Input-Addressed: If a comment in a build script changes, the input hash changes, forcing a rebuild even if the resulting binary is identical.
Content-Addressed (CA derivations): Nix verifies the cryptographic hash of the output. If two independent derivations produce the exact same binary, they share the exact same store path.

Source A ──► Compiles ──► Binary (Hash: X) ──► /nix/store/X-app
Source B ──► Compiles ──► Binary (Hash: X) ──► Reuses /nix/store/X-app!
This dramatically improves cache deduplication in large build farms.

title: Content-Addressable Paths
text:
Worked examples
Check path immutability:
Run:
touch $(which nix) 2>&1 || true
Output:
touch: cannot touch '/nix/store/...-nix-2.24.1/bin/nix': Permission denied
Store paths cannot be modified in place. Rebuilding with different contents produces a completely distinct hash.

title: Content-Addressable Paths
text:
The boring rule

Let Nix manage content addressing automatically.
Never attempt to force write access into the store.

title: Cryptographic Hashes and Inputs
text:
Cryptographic Hashes and Inputs
How does Nix guarantee that two machines compile the exact same binary? The boring default is: every input (source code, compiler version, patches, build script) is hashed, and any single-bit difference changes the output path.

title: Cryptographic Hashes and Inputs
text:
Mental model
Traditional package managers assume version numbers like v1.4.0 imply identity. In reality, a package compiled against glibc 2.38 behaves differently than one compiled against glibc 2.39.
Nix hashes the full input specification (the .drv file). If a compiler flag changes from -O2 to -O3, the hash changes, generating a separate, isolated store path.

title: Cryptographic Hashes and Inputs
text:
Worked examples
Check input hashes in derivation files:
Run:
nix-instantiate -E 'derivation { name = "sample"; builder = "/bin/sh"; system = builtins.currentSystem; }'
Output:
/nix/store/7vqw...-sample.drv
The derivation hash is calculated before a single line of compilation occurs.

title: Cryptographic Hashes and Inputs
text:
The boring rule

Every dependency is pinned by its cryptographic hash.
Upgrading a dependency creates a new path without mutating the existing one.

title: Deterministic Dynamic Linking and RPATH
text:
Deterministic Dynamic Linking and RPATH
Dynamic linking in traditional Linux is based on file names like libc.so.6. If that file is updated globally, every application on the host changes behavior simultaneously. The boring default of Nix is: embed the exact cryptographic hash of every required dependency into the binary’s runtime header (ELF RPATH).

title: Deterministic Dynamic Linking and RPATH
text:
Mental model
When Nix compiles a binary, it hardcodes the exact store path into the ELF header:
ELF Header (RUNPATH):
  /nix/store/7r44p...-glibc-2.39/lib
The dynamic linker looks strictly in that directory, ignoring /lib and /usr/lib.

title: Deterministic Dynamic Linking and RPATH
text:
Worked examples
Check the runtime path of an installed binary:
readelf -d $(which rg) | grep -E '(RPATH|RUNPATH)'
Output:
 0x000000000000001d (RUNPATH)            Library runpath: [/nix/store/7r44p12l4b72j9m9l09k96yghz02f8n7-glibc-2.39/lib]

title: Deterministic Dynamic Linking and RPATH
text:
The boring rule

Binaries embed explicit store paths via RUNPATH.
Never set global LD_LIBRARY_PATH variables.

title: Dependency Closures and Graphs
text:
Dependency Closures and Graphs
Every software artifact in Nix is a node in an immutable directed acyclic graph (DAG). The boring default is: distinguish build closures from runtime closures, and use nix-store -q --requisites to verify production deployment size.

title: Dependency Closures and Graphs
text:
Mental model

Build-Time Closure: Compilers, header files, and tools needed to produce the binary.
Runtime Closure: Only the files directly or transitively referenced by the finished binary.
Reference Scanning: Nix scans output files for string occurrences of store hashes. Unreferenced build tools are stripped from the runtime closure automatically.

title: Dependency Closures and Graphs
text:
Worked examples
Inspect the runtime closure of an executable:
Run:
nix-store -q --requisites $(which rg)
Output:
/nix/store/7r44p12l4b72j9m9l09k96yghz02f8n7-glibc-2.39
/nix/store/z1k947f6y788sfaivs931h26hsvb3506-ripgrep-14.1.0
Only these two store paths are required to run rg.

title: Dependency Closures and Graphs
text:
The boring rule

Query runtime closures with nix-store -q --requisites.
Trust reference scanning to drop build-time dependencies automatically.

title: The Nix Database (db.sqlite)
text:
The Nix Database (db.sqlite)
How does Nix know which store paths are valid and which packages refer to each other? The boring default is: Nix tracks all store registrations and reference relationships in a local SQLite database at /nix/var/nix/db/db.sqlite.

title: The Nix Database (db.sqlite)
text:
Mental model
The Nix store database records: 1. Valid Paths: Every store path successfully registered by a build or substitute. 2. References Graph: Direct references from one store path to another. 3. Derivers: Which .drv file produced a given store path.
/nix/store/
    ├── File tree (immutable files)
    └── /nix/var/nix/db/db.sqlite (registration & reference index)

title: The Nix Database (db.sqlite)
text:
Worked examples
Query referrers (which packages depend on a path):
nix-store -q --referrers $(which rg)
Output:
/nix/store/z1k947f6y788sfaivs931h26hsvb3506-ripgrep-14.1.0
Because nothing else references this specific ripgrep build, removing its profile symlink allows it to be garbage collected.

title: The Nix Database (db.sqlite)
text:
The boring rule

Never manually edit or lock /nix/var/nix/db/db.sqlite.
Use nix-store --verify --check-contents if you ever suspect filesystem corruption.

title: GC Roots and Space Reclamation
text:
GC Roots and Space Reclamation
Because Nix never overwrites existing packages, disk usage in /nix/store naturally grows over time. The boring default is: use garbage collector roots (gcroots) to preserve active environments, and run nix-collect-garbage to clean unreferenced paths.

title: GC Roots and Space Reclamation
text:
Mental model

GC Roots: Pointers that tell the garbage collector “do not delete this path”.
Roots Locations:

System generations (/nix/var/nix/profiles/system-link)
User profile generations (~/.nix-profile)
Local build symlinks (result registered in /nix/var/nix/gcroots/auto)

Dead Paths: Any store path with zero references from any GC root is eligible for deletion.

title: GC Roots and Space Reclamation
text:
Worked examples
Run garbage collection safely:
nix-collect-garbage
Output:
finding garbage collector roots...
deleting garbage...
14 store paths deleted, 142.50 MiB freed
This cleans unreferenced, orphaned files while keeping rollback generations intact.

title: GC Roots and Space Reclamation
text:
The boring rule

Always delete packages via nix-collect-garbage, never with manual rm.
Use nix-collect-garbage -d to delete older generations and reclaim space.

title: Store Optimization and Deduplication
text:
Store Optimization and Deduplication
When multiple package versions share identical files (like licenses, shared headers, or static assets), duplicate copies waste disk space. The boring default is: use hard-link deduplication via nix-store --optimise to replace duplicate files with shared physical inodes.

title: Store Optimization and Deduplication
text:
Mental model
Unlike traditional filesystems where identical files across packages consume double the space: - Nix verifies SHA-256 hashes of individual files. - When identical content is found, it links both paths to the same disk inode. - The files remain independent and read-only.
/nix/store/pkgA/lib/data.bin (Inode 1001) ──┐
                                            ├──► Shared Physical Disk Block
/nix/store/pkgB/lib/data.bin (Inode 1001) ──┘

title: Store Optimization and Deduplication
text:
Worked examples
Run store optimization:
nix-store --optimise
Output:
hashing files in /nix/store...
31420 files linked, 850.40 MiB freed
Gigabytes of redundant disk space are reclaimed without modifying or rebuilding packages.

title: Store Optimization and Deduplication
text:
The boring rule

Run nix-store --optimise periodically or enable nix.optimise.automatic = true; in NixOS.
Deduplication is safe because the store is read-only.

title: The Derivation Primitive
text:
The Derivation Primitive
At the lowest level, Nix builds packages using the built-in function derivation.
A derivation requires three mandatory attributes: 1. name: A string identifier. 2. system: The target architecture string ("x86_64-linux", "aarch64-darwin"). 3. builder: The path to the executable executing the build (usually /bin/sh).

title: The Derivation Primitive
The Derivation Primitive
text:
The boring rule

A derivation is a pure function evaluated into a .drv file and realized as a store path.

title: Building Multi-File Artifacts
text:
Building Multi-File Artifacts
Derivations can produce complete directory hierarchies with executables, configuration files, and documentation.

title: Building Multi-File Artifacts
text:
Mental model
The $out variable provided by the builder does not have to be a single file. You can create $out/bin, $out/lib, and $out/share to package complete applications.

title: Building Multi-File Artifacts
text:
Worked examples
Save as multifile.nix:
# multifile.nix
derivation {
  name = "desk-assets";
  system = builtins.currentSystem;
  builder = "/bin/sh";
  args = [
    "-c"
    ''
      mkdir -p $out/bin $out/share
      echo '#!/bin/sh' > $out/bin/desk-status
      echo 'echo status: ready' >> $out/bin/desk-status
      chmod +x $out/bin/desk-status
      echo 'Desk version 1.0' > $out/share/version.txt
    ''
  ];
}
Run:
nix-build multifile.nix
Output:
/nix/store/99ka...-desk-assets
Test the generated script:
./result/bin/desk-status
Output:
status: ready

title: Building Multi-File Artifacts
text:
The boring rule

Always create the target directories (mkdir -p $out/bin) before writing outputs.
Test outputs locally by running ./result/bin/....

title: Nix Expressions and Evaluation
text:
Nix Expressions and Evaluation
Nix does not execute a sequential list of statements; it evaluates a single tree of pure expressions. The boring default is: every file is a single expression yielding a value, pure evaluation produces identical results regardless of when or where it is run, and lazy evaluation computes only what is accessed.

title: Nix Expressions and Evaluation
text:
Mental model
In imperative scripting languages (Python, Bash), code executes step-by-step from top to bottom, altering environment variables and writing to global state.
In Nix: 1. Pure Expression Model: There are no statements, no variable mutations, and no global side effects. 2 + 2 is an expression; { a = 1; } is an expression; a 500-line package definition is a single expression. 2. Deterministic Evaluation: Given identical inputs, evaluating an expression will always yield the exact same AST and data structure. 3. Lazy Evaluation: Nix expressions are evaluated only when their values are needed for a build or terminal output. If you define 50 attribute keys but only query myConfig.port, the other 49 expressions are never computed.
Imperative (Bash/Python):
  Step 1 -> Mutate state -> Step 2 -> Mutate state -> Final state (Stateful)

Pure Expression (Nix):
  Root Expression -> Evaluates sub-expressions lazily -> Computed Value (Deterministic)

title: Nix Expressions and Evaluation
Nix Expressions and Evaluation
text:
The trap
Expecting side effects like echo or file writes to occur during Nix evaluation. Nix expressions evaluate purely in memory; the only file writes occur during the sandboxed build phase of derivations.
The fix: Use Nix expressions to generate pure data and configuration structures; let builders and systemd modules perform physical execution.

title: Nix Expressions and Evaluation
text:
The boring rule

Every .nix file must evaluate to exactly one expression.
Rely on laziness: you can declare large configurations without paying an evaluation penalty for unused branches.
Use nix eval --expr for quick scratchpad calculations and syntax experiments.

title: Nix Expressions and Evaluation
text:
Try this

Evaluate an attribute selection on laziness_proof.nix that forces brokenField to be read (nix eval --file laziness_proof.nix brokenField) and observe the throw error.

title: Values and Immutability
text:
Values and Immutability
In Nix, values cannot be altered once constructed. The boring default is: understand that all data in Nix is deeply immutable, transformations always yield fresh values, and lexical scopes eliminate state corruption.

title: Values and Immutability
text:
Mental model
In traditional languages, mutability creates complex bugs:
# Python mutable bug:
config = {"port": 8080}
mutate_config(config) # modifies original dictionary in place!
In Nix: 1. Values are Immutable: Once an attribute set, list, or string is defined, it can never be modified. 2. Transformations are Pure: Merging an attribute set with // or adding items to a list with ++ does not modify the original data structure; it allocates a new value representing the result. 3. Thread Safety & Cacheability: Because values cannot change under your feet, the Nix evaluator and binary caches can safely memoize and reuse values indefinitely.
Original Value ({ a = 1; }) ───┐
                               ├──► New Result ({ a = 1; b = 2; })
Update ({ b = 2; }) ───────────┘
(Original remains unchanged: { a = 1; })

title: Values and Immutability
Values and Immutability
text:
The trap
Trying to assign to a previously bound name:
let
  x = 1;
  x = 2; # Syntax error!
in
x
Nix disallows multiple bindings of the same name in the same scope.
The fix: Use distinct descriptive names (initialConfig, productionConfig) or use child let blocks for local shadowing.

title: Values and Immutability
text:
The boring rule

Every data structure in Nix is immutable.
Merging attribute sets (//) and lists (++) always yields new values.
Immutability guarantees zero race conditions and perfect caching.

title: Values and Immutability
text:
Try this

Verify in nix repl that let a = { x = 1; }; b = a // { x = 2; }; in a.x evaluates to 1.

title: Data Types and String Interpolation
text:
Data Types and String Interpolation
Nix is dynamically typed with strict type checking at runtime. The boring default is: understand primitive types (integers, floats, booleans, strings, paths, and null) and master ${...} string interpolation for safe configuration generation.

title: Data Types and String Interpolation
text:
Mental model
Nix has six primitive types: 1. Integers (int): 64-bit signed integers (42, -10). 2. Floats (float): IEEE 754 floating-point numbers (3.1415). 3. Booleans (bool): true or false. 4. Strings (string): UTF-8 encoded text ("hello" or multi-line ''hello''). 5. Paths (path): File paths beginning with /, ./, or ~/ (./config.nix). 6. Null (null): Represents the intentional absence of a value.
String interpolation ${expression} embeds any expression that evaluates to a string, number, or path directly into a string.
"Server: ${host}:${toString port}"
When a path is interpolated into a string inside a derivation, Nix copies that file into /nix/store and substitutes its cryptographic store path.

title: Data Types and String Interpolation
Data Types and String Interpolation
text:
The trap
Interpolating non-string values like integers without converting them first. Writing "${42}" in raw Nix fails because integers cannot be coerced to strings implicitly.
The fix: Always wrap numbers with toString: "${toString port}".

title: Data Types and String Interpolation
text:
The boring rule

Convert integers to strings with toString before interpolating.
Use unquoted paths (./config.json) when you want Nix to track and store the file.
Use double single quotes ('') for multi-line bash scripts and systemd units.

title: Data Types and String Interpolation
text:
Try this

In nix repl, test builtins.typeOf (toString 42) and verify it returns "string".

title: Let-In Blocks and Local Bindings
text:
Let-In Blocks and Local Bindings
Nix does not have mutable assignment statements. The boring default is: use let ... in ... to introduce clear, locally-scoped, immutable bindings that make complex expressions readable.

title: Let-In Blocks and Local Bindings
text:
Mental model
The let ... in construct has two sections: - let: A block of bindings in the form name = expression;. - in: The expression that is evaluated, in which those bindings are accessible.
Bindings inside a let block are mutually recursive by default: a binding can reference any other binding in the same block, regardless of line order.
let
  b = a + 10;
  a = 5;
in
b  # evaluates to 15
Evaluation order is driven by dependency need, not textual sequence.

title: Let-In Blocks and Local Bindings
Let-In Blocks and Local Bindings
text:
The trap
Creating massive 200-line let blocks containing unrelated helpers. When a let block grows too large, readability degrades.
The fix: Group related helpers into separate .nix files and bring them in with import.

title: Let-In Blocks and Local Bindings
text:
The boring rule

Use let ... in to name intermediate calculations and keep expressions clean.
Use inherit to avoid redundant key = key; syntax.
Remember bindings are evaluated lazily: unused let bindings incur zero runtime cost.

title: Let-In Blocks and Local Bindings
text:
Try this

In desk_service.nix, add an unused binding unused = throw "never evaluated"; and verify that evaluation still succeeds because of laziness.

title: Functions and Argument Defaults
text:
Functions and Argument Defaults
Functions in Nix are first-class values that take exactly one argument and return a value. The boring default is: accept a single attribute set with explicit destructuring, supply sane default values with ?, and use ... only when wrapping extensible APIs.

title: Functions and Argument Defaults
text:
Mental model
Nix function syntax uses a colon : separating the argument pattern from the function body:
x: x + 1
For functions requiring multiple parameters, there are two patterns: 1. Currying: x: y: x + y 2. Attribute Set Destructuring (The standard): { name, port ? 8080, ... }: ...
Destructuring allows named parameters in any order, optional defaults (? default), and extra attribute tolerance (...).

title: Functions and Argument Defaults
Functions and Argument Defaults
text:
The trap
Omitting ... when a function receives configuration from external modules. If an unexpected attribute is passed without ..., evaluation halts immediately with an “unexpected argument” error.
The fix: Use ... at the end of parameter sets for open/extensible interfaces (like package and module declarations).

title: Functions and Argument Defaults
text:
The boring rule

Always prefer attribute set destructuring ({ pkgs, lib, ... }:) over curried functions for configuration code.
Provide sensible defaults with ? default.
Use inherit inside functions to assemble result sets cleanly.

title: Attribute Sets and Recursive Definitions
text:
Attribute Sets and Recursive Definitions
Attribute sets are the workhorse data structure of Nix. The boring default is: use standard attribute sets, merge them with //, access fields with dot-notation (a.b.c), and reserve rec for simple, acyclic sibling references.

title: Attribute Sets and Recursive Definitions
text:
Mental model
An attribute set is a collection of key-value pairs wrapped in braces:
{ key1 = "value1"; key2 = 42; }
Key operations: 1. Dot Access: set.key1 2. Fallback Operator (or): set.missingKey or "default" 3. Merge Operator (//): { a = 1; b = 2; } // { b = 3; c = 4; } (right-hand side overwrites left) 4. Nested Syntax: desk.database.port = 5432; is equivalent to desk = { database = { port = 5432; }; }; 5. Recursive Attribute Sets (rec): Allows attributes within the set to reference other attributes in the same set.

title: Attribute Sets and Recursive Definitions
Attribute Sets and Recursive Definitions
text:
The trap
Using rec and then overriding a key with //. Overriding a field in a rec set does not automatically update other fields that referenced the original value.
# Anti-pattern: expecting // to update references in rec
let
  base = rec { x = 1; y = x + 1; };
  updated = base // { x = 10; };
in
updated.y # Still evaluates to 2, not 11!
The fix: Use functions (makeConfig = { x, ... }: ...) or let ... in blocks when you need values to propagate after overrides.

title: Attribute Sets and Recursive Definitions
text:
The boring rule

Use a.b.c or default for safe property access.
Use // for shallow configuration overrides.
Use rec only when the set is self-contained and will not be extended or overridden with //.

title: Conditionals, Lists, and Built-in Operations
text:
Conditionals, Lists, and Built-in Operations
Transforming collections and applying conditional flags are common when configuring systems. The boring default is: use standard if ... then ... else ... expressions, concatenate lists with ++, and leverage builtins.map and builtins.filter for pure transformations.

title: Conditionals, Lists, and Built-in Operations
text:
Mental model

Conditionals: In Nix, if is an expression that yields a value, not a control-flow statement. The else clause is mandatory:
if condition then valueA else valueB
Lists: Space-separated elements wrapped in square brackets:
[ 1 "two" ./three (4 + 5) ]
List Concatenation: Using ++:
[ 1 2 ] ++ [ 3 4 ] # evaluates to [ 1 2 3 4 ]
Built-in Pure Operations: Functions provided by the Nix runtime under builtins, including builtins.map, builtins.filter, builtins.length, and builtins.elem.

title: Conditionals, Lists, and Built-in Operations
Conditionals, Lists, and Built-in Operations
text:
The trap
Forgetting the else clause in an if expression. Because Nix is purely functional, an if expression without an else has no defined fallback value and produces a syntax error.
The fix: Always supply both then and else branches. If you want an attribute to be conditionally omitted, use lib.optionalAttrs or lib.mkIf.

title: Conditionals, Lists, and Built-in Operations
text:
The boring rule

Every if must have an else.
Use ++ to combine lists.
Rely on built-ins (builtins.map, builtins.filter) for standard collection processing.

title: Importing Files and Building Abstractions
text:
Importing Files and Building Abstractions
Real systems cannot fit inside a single .nix file. The boring default is: split logic into small, modular files, pass explicit arguments into them, and import them with the import operator.

title: Importing Files and Building Abstractions
text:
Mental model
In Nix, import is a built-in function that takes a path to a .nix file and evaluates it:
import ./constants.nix
If the imported file evaluates to a function, you pass arguments immediately:
import ./service.nix { inherit pkgs; port = 8080; }
There are no circular dependencies, hidden global namespaces, or implicit module registries. An imported file only has access to what is explicitly passed into it.

title: Importing Files and Building Abstractions
Importing Files and Building Abstractions
text:
The trap
Importing files that rely on ambient path lookups like <nixpkgs> in production configurations. <nixpkgs> depends on the host machine’s $NIX_PATH channel, reintroducing non-reproducibility across different machines.
The fix: Pin dependencies using Flakes or explicit pinned tarball URLs (builtins.fetchTarball).

title: Importing Files and Building Abstractions
text:
The boring rule

Structure large configurations as directories of focused .nix files.
Each .nix file should return a function accepting its dependencies ({ lib, config, ... }:).
Keep file boundaries clear and avoid deeply nested abstractions.

title: Nix Shells and the devShell Concept
text:
Nix Shells and the devShell Concept
Development environments rot when developers install tools directly onto their host machines. The boring default is: define a shell.nix or devShell declaring the exact tools required, and activate it with nix-shell or nix develop.

title: Nix Shells and the devShell Concept
text:
Mental model
A Nix devShell is an ephemeral execution environment: 1. It downloads or builds only the packages listed in packages or buildInputs. 2. It sets up $PATH, environment variables, and compiler flags in a child shell. 3. It does not alter your workstation’s global system directories. 4. When you exit the shell (exit or Ctrl+D), your environment reverts instantly to normal.
Host OS ($PATH = /usr/bin)
  │
  ├── nix-shell starts
  │     └── Injects /nix/store/abc...-go-1.27/bin into $PATH
  │     └── Runs shellHook
  │     └── Developer compiles and tests
  │
  └── exit drops back to pristine Host OS ($PATH = /usr/bin)

title: Nix Shells and the devShell Concept
Nix Shells and the devShell Concept
text:
The trap
Installing development compilers like Go, Rust, or Node globally with system package managers (apt, brew). Different projects inevitably require different versions, leading to version conflicts.
The fix: Use a shell.nix in each repository.

title: Nix Shells and the devShell Concept
text:
The boring rule

Every project repository must have a root shell.nix or flake.nix.
Use pkgs.mkShell with packages for modern shells.
Use shellHook for local environment configuration and diagnostics.

title: Nix Shells and the devShell Concept
text:
Try this

Add pkgs.tree to shell.nix and run nix-shell --run "tree -L 1".

title: Multi-Language Development Environments
text:
Multi-Language Development Environments
Modern systems frequently combine multiple languages: a Go backend, a TypeScript frontend, Python data scripts, and C shared libraries. The boring default is: declare all runtimes, compilers, and library headers inside a single unified mkShell definition.

title: Multi-Language Development Environments
text:
Mental model
In traditional systems, managing polyglot stacks requires coordinating multiple independent version managers (asdf, nvm, pyenv, rustup) and installing system development packages (libssl-dev, libpq-dev).
Nix unifies this: - Compilers (go, rustc, nodejs) are just packages. - C libraries (openssl, postgresql) provide headers and shared objects automatically. - pkg-config is wired up automatically when included in nativeBuildInputs.

title: Multi-Language Development Environments
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Unified Polyglot Stack
Save as polyglot.nix.
# polyglot.nix
{ pkgs ? import <nixpkgs> {} }:

pkgs.mkShell {
  packages = [
    pkgs.go
    pkgs.nodejs_22
    (pkgs.python3.withPackages (ps: [ ps.requests ps.pydantic ]))
    pkgs.sqlite
  ];

  shellHook = ''
    echo "Polyglot environment loaded: Go, Node, Python, SQLite"
  '';
}
Run:
nix-shell polyglot.nix --run "go version && node --version && python3 --version"
Output:
Polyglot environment loaded: Go, Node, Python, SQLite
go version go1.27.1 linux/amd64
v22.11.0
Python 3.12.7
All runtimes coexist without path or library collision.


Case 2: C Libraries and pkg-config
Save as native_c.nix. A shell that configures C headers and libraries for applications that compile native extensions.
# native_c.nix
{ pkgs ? import <nixpkgs> {} }:

pkgs.mkShell {
  nativeBuildInputs = [ pkgs.pkg-config ];
  buildInputs = [ pkgs.openssl pkgs.zlib ];

  shellHook = ''
    echo "OpenSSL cflags: $(pkg-config --cflags openssl)"
  '';
}
Run:
nix-shell native_c.nix --run "echo C libraries configured"
Output:
OpenSSL cflags: -I/nix/store/...-openssl-3.3.2-dev/include
C libraries configured
pkg-config points directly to the isolated store header directories.

title: Multi-Language Development Environments
text:
The trap
Relying on host system header files like /usr/include/openssl. If a teammate is on a different Linux distribution or macOS, paths differ and builds fail.
The fix: Always include header and library dependencies explicitly in buildInputs.

title: Multi-Language Development Environments
text:
The boring rule

Group build-time tools (like pkg-config, cmake) in nativeBuildInputs.
Group runtime libraries and headers (like openssl, zlib) in buildInputs.
Use language-specific package wrappers (like python3.withPackages).

title: Flakes for Reproducible Dev Environments
text:
Flakes for Reproducible Dev Environments
Classic shell.nix still relies on <nixpkgs>, which can vary across developer machines depending on their channel state. The boring default is: use modern Nix Flakes (flake.nix + flake.lock) to pin the exact commit of nixpkgs across the entire team.

title: Flakes for Reproducible Dev Environments
text:
Mental model
Nix Flakes introduce three critical improvements: 1. Pinned Lockfiles (flake.lock): Automatically records the exact Git commit hash of every dependency. 2. Standard Output Schema: Predictable structure (packages.${system}, devShells.${system}.default). 3. Pure Evaluation: Flakes disallow reading undeclared files, ambient environment variables, or mutable network channels.
flake.nix (declares inputs & outputs)
    │
    ▼
flake.lock (records exact Git commit of nixpkgs)
    │
    ▼
nix develop (creates identical shell on all machines)

title: Flakes for Reproducible Dev Environments
Flakes for Reproducible Dev Environments
text:
The trap
Forgetting to check flake.lock into Git. Without flake.lock, teammates generate their own lockfiles on different dates, losing strict bit-for-bit reproducibility.
The fix: Always commit flake.lock alongside flake.nix.

title: Flakes for Reproducible Dev Environments
text:
The boring rule

Always use Flakes for new development environments.
Always commit flake.lock to source control.
Use nix develop to enter Flake-based development shells.

title: Flakes for Reproducible Dev Environments
text:
Try this

Inspect flake.lock with cat flake.lock or jq . flake.lock and locate the rev (revision) field.

title: Environment Management with Home Manager
text:
Environment Management with Home Manager
Project-specific devShells provide tools for a specific repository, but developers also need personal utilities across all shells (Git configurations, shell prompts, editor settings). The boring default is: use Home Manager to manage user-level tools and configuration files declaratively.

title: Environment Management with Home Manager
text:
Mental model
Home Manager applies the Nix module system to the user’s home directory ($HOME): 1. User Packages (home.packages): Installs CLI tools into ~/.nix-profile without requiring root permissions. 2. Managed Dotfiles: Generates read-only symlinks in ~/.config/ pointing to /nix/store paths. 3. Integration with devShells: Personal utilities (like your favorite shell prompt, tmux bindings, and Git aliases) remain active globally, while project-specific compilers and libraries are injected on top via devShell.
User Space ($HOME)
  ├── Managed by Home Manager (git, zsh, vim, starship prompt)
  └── Inside Project Directory:
        └── Activated devShell adds project Go 1.27 and Postgres CLI

title: Environment Management with Home Manager
Environment Management with Home Manager
text:
The trap
Using Home Manager to install project-specific language runtimes (e.g., globally pinning Go 1.27 in home.packages). When another project requires Go 1.26, global conflicts return.
The fix: Reserve Home Manager for personal user utilities. Keep compilers and language libraries inside project devShells.

title: Environment Management with Home Manager
text:
The boring rule

Home Manager manages user preferences and personal CLI tools.
Project repositories manage their own compilers and runtimes via devShell.
Keep dotfiles version-controlled in Git.

title: Migrating from Docker Desktop to Nix DevShells
text:
Migrating from Docker Desktop to Nix DevShells
Many teams default to running basic development tools inside Docker containers to avoid dependency drift. The boring default is: migrate local development toolchains to native Nix devShells for near-zero startup latency, direct editor integration, and fractional resource consumption.

title: Migrating from Docker Desktop to Nix DevShells
text:
Mental model








Dimension
Docker Desktop Container
Nix devShell




Architecture
Linux VM + Container Daemon
Native Host Process


Startup Latency
5 – 20 seconds
< 50 milliseconds


File I/O Performance
Slow across VM bind-mounts
Native host filesystem speed


IDE Integration
Requires Remote-Containers plugins
Direct local LSP & debugger integration


Resource Usage
4 – 8 GB RAM continuously
Exact binary memory only when executed



Containers remain the right choice for isolated services (e.g. running an actual PostgreSQL database or Redis instance). They are the wrong choice for running simple compilers (go, rustc, npm).

title: Migrating from Docker Desktop to Nix DevShells
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: The Docker Compose Pattern vs The Nix devShell Pattern
Compare a typical docker-compose.yml with a clean flake.nix.
Docker setup requires bind mounts, ports, and a persistent background VM.
The Nix equivalent:
Save as flake.nix:
# flake.nix
{
  description = "Fast native desk development environment";

  inputs.nixpkgs.url = "github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-24.11";

  outputs = { self, nixpkgs }:
    let
      pkgs = import nixpkgs { system = "x86_64-linux"; };
    in
    {
      devShells.x86_64-linux.default = pkgs.mkShell {
        packages = [
          pkgs.go
          pkgs.golangci-lint
          pkgs.delve
        ];
      };
    };
}
Run:
nix develop --command go test ./...
Output:
ok      desk/service    0.015s
Compilation and tests run at native host speed without VM translation layers or volume-mount caching slowdowns.


Case 2: Hybrid Workflow — Native Tooling with Containerized Backends
The recommended production pattern: - Language toolchains & linters: Run natively via Nix devShell. - Stateful databases & caches: Run as lightweight containers via Podman or Docker.
Save as start_services.sh:
# start_services.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

echo "Launching isolated database container..."
podman run -d --name desk-db -p 5432:5432 -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret postgres:16-alpine || true

echo "Running migrations with native Nix-provided toolchain:"
psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U postgres -c "SELECT 'Desk database online' AS status;"
Run:
nix-shell -p postgresql --run "bash start_services.sh"
Output:
Launching isolated database container...
Running migrations with native Nix-provided toolchain:
        status        
----------------------
 Desk database online
(1 row)
The CLI tools are provided instantly by Nix; the database runs isolated in a container.

title: Migrating from Docker Desktop to Nix DevShells
text:
The trap
Running full GUI editors or IDEs inside containers or remote VMs when simple local toolchain isolation is all that was needed.
The fix: Use Nix to provide the compilers and tools on your host OS. Your editor connects directly to native binaries on $PATH.

title: Migrating from Docker Desktop to Nix DevShells
text:
The boring rule

Use Nix devShells for compilers, language servers, CLI tools, and linters.
Reserve containers for long-running stateful services (databases, message queues).
Enjoy native host file I/O speed and seamless editor integration.

title: The Nix Package Manager in Practice
text:
The Nix Package Manager in Practice
The Nix package manager allows managing software without root access, side effects, or system collisions. The boring default is: use nix profile for persistent CLI tools on your user profile, use nix shell for one-off trials, and inspect package attributes via nix search.

title: The Nix Package Manager in Practice
text:
Mental model
Unlike traditional package managers that overwrite files in /usr/bin, the Nix package manager manages packages as symlink generations in user profiles (~/.nix-profile pointing to /nix/var/nix/profiles/per-user/$USER/profile).
Key command patterns: 1. One-Off Trial (nix shell nixpkgs#htop): Drops you into a temporary subshell with htop available on $PATH. Exiting removes it from your environment without leaving debris. 2. Persistent Tooling (nix profile install nixpkgs#ripgrep): Installs a tool into your personal user profile. Creates a new rollback generation. 3. Rollback (nix profile rollback): Instantly reverts your installed CLI packages to the previous generation if an update misbehaves. 4. Search (nix search nixpkgs <query>): Queries package names and descriptions across the pinned flake or channel registry.

title: The Nix Package Manager in Practice
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Ephemeral CLI Execution with nix shell
Run an interactive utility without permanently installing it.
Run:
nix shell nixpkgs#cowsay --command cowsay "Desk system ready"
Output:
 ____________________
< Desk system ready >
 --------------------
        \   ^__^
         \  (oo)\_______
            (__)\       )\/\
                ||----w |
                ||     ||
cowsay was fetched, mounted to $PATH, executed, and unmounted. Your system remains untouched.


Case 2: User Profile Management with nix profile
Install and manage tools persistently in your user profile.
Run:
nix profile install nixpkgs#jq
Output:
[1 added]
List active packages in your profile:
nix profile list
Output:
Index:              0
Flake attribute:    packages.x86_64-linux.jq
Package name:       jq
Store paths:        /nix/store/a1b2c...-jq-1.7.1


Case 3: Rollback in Action
Simulate rolling back an installation.
Run:
nix profile rollback
Output:
switching to generation 1
Generations are atomic and instantaneous.

title: The Nix Package Manager in Practice
text:
The trap
Using nix-env -iA from legacy Nix workflows. nix-env creates unpinned, unmanaged profile mutations that conflict easily with modern Flakes.
The fix: Use modern nix profile or declare tools systematically with Home Manager or devShell.

title: The Nix Package Manager in Practice
text:
The boring rule

Use nix shell nixpkgs#pkg when you need a tool for 5 minutes.
Use nix profile for user-level tools that persist across terminal tabs.
Use nix profile history and nix profile rollback when diagnosing tool regressions.

title: Understanding the Flakes Input System
text:
Understanding the Flakes Input System
Managing multi-repository dependencies without version skew requires an explicit lockfile standard. The boring default is: declare all external Git repositories and Nix libraries inside inputs, override shared inputs with inputs.<name>.follows, and let flake.lock ensure strict reproducibility.

title: Understanding the Flakes Input System
Understanding the Flakes Input System
Understanding the Flakes Input System
text:
The trap
Neglecting to use follows for large dependencies. If three external flakes each pull their own independent branch of nixpkgs, your build tree evaluates nixpkgs three times and downloads gigabytes of duplicate compilers and glibc packages.
The fix: Always configure inputs.<dep>.inputs.nixpkgs.follows = "nixpkgs";.

title: Understanding the Flakes Input System
text:
The boring rule

Always specify exact release branches (nixos-24.11), not unconstrained master.
Use follows to consolidate nixpkgs across all flake dependencies.
Commit flake.lock to Git and update with nix flake update deliberately.

title: Understanding the Flakes Input System
text:
Try this

title: Creating and Composing Overlays
text:
Creating and Composing Overlays
Standard packages from nixpkgs often need a patch, a compiler flag, or a specific custom version. The boring default is: use an overlay (final: prev: { ... }) to customize packages cleanly without forking upstream repositories.

title: Creating and Composing Overlays
Creating and Composing Overlays
Creating and Composing Overlays
text:
The trap
Using final instead of prev when overriding a package (final.pkg.overrideAttrs ...). This creates a circular dependency where the package attempts to override itself, causing an infinite recursion error during evaluation.
The fix: Always use prev.package.override or prev.package.overrideAttrs. Use final only when referencing other packages.

title: Creating and Composing Overlays
text:
The boring rule

Always write overlays with signature final: prev: { ... }.
Use prev to reference the package you are overriding.
Use final when referring to sibling dependencies.
Keep overlays in standalone files (overlays/my-package.nix) and import them into nixpkgs.overlays.

title: Custom Package Definitions
text:
Custom Package Definitions
Every team eventually needs to package internal services, proprietary CLI tools, or unmaintained upstream libraries. The boring default is: write a package recipe as a function accepting { lib, stdenv, fetchFromGitHub, ... }, and instantiate it using callPackage.

title: Custom Package Definitions
text:
Mental model
The idiomatic way to define packages in Nix is the callPackage pattern: 1. The Recipe (package.nix): A pure function declaring its build and runtime dependencies as arguments. 2. Dependency Injection (callPackage ./package.nix {}): Inspects the arguments of the recipe and automatically supplies matching packages from pkgs. 3. Clean Overrides: Callers can override specific arguments by passing them in the second set: callPackage ./package.nix { enableFeature = true; }.
pkgs.callPackage
     │
     ├── Reads arguments of package.nix: { stdenv, curl, jq }
     ├── Automatically injects pkgs.stdenv, pkgs.curl, pkgs.jq
     └── Returns evaluated derivation

title: Custom Package Definitions
Custom Package Definitions
text:
The trap
Hardcoding pkgs.curl and pkgs.jq directly inside your package recipe instead of accepting them as function arguments. This prevents other developers from overriding dependencies, cross-compiling, or substituting security patches.
The fix: Always use the callPackage pattern: declare dependencies in the function header { lib, stdenv, curl, jq }: and let Nix inject them.

title: Custom Package Definitions
text:
The boring rule

Every custom package file must be a function taking dependencies as arguments.
Use pkgs.callPackage ./path.nix {} to instantiate package definitions.
Use wrapProgram to ensure runtime shell scripts find their CLI dependencies deterministically.

title: Custom Package Definitions
text:
Try this

In default.nix, override a dependency explicitly: pkgs.callPackage ./desk-tool.nix { curl = pkgs.curl.override { ... }; }.

title: Managing Dependencies Across Projects
text:
Managing Dependencies Across Projects
Organizations operate multiple internal repositories that share packages, libraries, and linters. The boring default is: export packages, overlays, and devShells as a central organizational Flake, and import them across projects with locked version pins.

title: Managing Dependencies Across Projects
text:
Mental model
In legacy ecosystems, teams build internal Debian packages, maintain private Docker registries, or duplicate boilerplate bash scripts across every repository.
With Nix Flakes: 1. Central Infrastructure Flake (github:org/desk-infra): Packages internal libraries, database migration tools, and custom linters. Exports them as packages and overlays. 2. Consuming Repositories: Declare the central infrastructure flake in their inputs. 3. Lockfile Guarantee: Each consuming project updates its reference to the internal flake via nix flake update desk-infra deliberately, preventing unexpected breakages when internal tooling is updated.
Internal Repo: org/desk-tooling (Flake)
        │
        ├── Exports packages.x86_64-linux.desk-cli
        ├── Exports overlays.default
        │
        ▼
Consuming Repo: org/billing-service (Flake)
        └── inputs.desk-tooling.url = "github:org/desk-tooling";
        └── Uses desk-cli in devShells.default

title: Managing Dependencies Across Projects
Managing Dependencies Across Projects
text:
The trap
Distributing internal tools via untracked curl scripts or mutable URLs. If an internal tool changes without a lockfile, unrelated project builds and CI pipelines fail unpredictably.
The fix: Distribute internal tools as Flakes with cryptographic lockfiles.

title: Managing Dependencies Across Projects
text:
The boring rule

Publish shared company tools, scripts, and linters in a dedicated Flake repository.
Export both packages and an overlays.default attribute.
Consuming projects pin the central flake in inputs with inputs.nixpkgs.follows.

title: Managing Dependencies Across Projects
text:

title: The Derivation Build Process
text:
The Derivation Build Process
At the core of Nix’s building capability is stdenv.mkDerivation. The boring default is: understand the standard build phases (unpack, patch, configure, build, check, install), override only the specific phases you need, and let stdenv manage compiler flags and sandboxing.

title: The Derivation Build Process
text:
Mental model
stdenv.mkDerivation wraps standard Unix build patterns into discrete phases: 1. unpackPhase: Unpacks $src into a temporary build directory. 2. patchPhase: Applies patch files listed in patches. 3. configurePhase: Runs ./configure --prefix=$out or builds CMake setup. 4. buildPhase: Runs make (or language equivalent). 5. checkPhase: Runs test suites (when doCheck = true;). 6. installPhase: Runs make install copying files to $out. 7. fixupPhase: Patches ELF RPATHs, strips debug symbols, and shrinks closures.
Source Archive ($src)
      │
      ├── unpackPhase ──► patchPhase ──► configurePhase
      │                                       │
      ▼                                       ▼
  installPhase ◄── checkPhase ◄── buildPhase
      │
      └── fixupPhase (patchelf, stripping) ──► Final $out in /nix/store

title: The Derivation Build Process
The Derivation Build Process
text:
The trap
Overwriting installPhase and forgetting to create $out before copying (mkdir -p $out/bin). If the directory does not exist, cp fails immediately.
The fix: Always ensure $out/bin or the target subdirectory is created in installPhase.

title: The Derivation Build Process
text:
The boring rule

Rely on standard phases; override only what is necessary (buildPhase, installPhase).
Set dontConfigure = true; or dontBuild = true; when skipping standard steps.
Enable tests during package build with doCheck = true;.

title: The Derivation Build Process
text:
Try this

In c_tool.nix, add checkPhase = "./desk-status-c"; doCheck = true; and verify tests run during nix-build.

title: Building C and C++ Projects with CMake
text:
Building C and C++ Projects with CMake
C and C++ projects typically use CMake for build configuration. The boring default is: add pkgs.cmake to nativeBuildInputs and let stdenv configure, compile, and install with standard flags automatically.

title: Building C and C++ Projects with CMake
text:
Mental model
In Nix, CMake is a first-class build tool: 1. Adding cmake to nativeBuildInputs activates Nix’s built-in CMake hook. 2. The hook automatically configures -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=$out and standard optimization flags. 3. You do not write manual cmake -B build commands; configurePhase and buildPhase handle it.
stdenv.mkDerivation
      └── nativeBuildInputs = [ cmake ];
            └── Automatically runs:
                  cmake -B build -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=$out
                  cmake --build build
                  cmake --install build

title: Building C and C++ Projects with CMake
Building C and C++ Projects with CMake
text:
The trap
Manually writing cmake -B build in buildPhase. This overrides the automatic prefix setup and flags configured by the Nix CMake setup hook.
The fix: Let stdenv execute configurePhase automatically; pass custom CMake options via cmakeFlags = [ "-DENABLE_FEATURE=ON" ];.

title: Building C and C++ Projects with CMake
text:
The boring rule

Put cmake in nativeBuildInputs (it is a build-time compiler tool).
Pass options using cmakeFlags = [ "-DFLAG=VALUE" ];.
Let stdenv handle configure, build, and install phases.

title: Building C and C++ Projects with CMake

title: Rust Packages with Cargo
text:
Rust Packages with Cargo
Rust projects use Cargo and Cargo.lock for deterministic dependency management. The boring default is: use pkgs.rustPlatform.buildRustPackage with cargoLock.lockFile to build hermetic Rust binaries without network access during compilation.

title: Rust Packages with Cargo
text:
Mental model
Nix builds are sandboxed and cannot access crates.io during compilation. buildRustPackage solves this with a two-step derivation: 1. Vendor Derivation (cargoLock): Downloads and vendors all crates declared in Cargo.lock into a fixed-output store path. 2. Build Derivation: Compiles the application completely offline using the vendored dependencies.
Cargo.lock ──► Fixed-Output Derivation (vendors crates) ──► cargo build --offline ──► $out/bin

title: Rust Packages with Cargo
Rust Packages with Cargo
text:
The trap
Using legacy cargoSha256 instead of modern cargoLock.lockFile. cargoSha256 requires updating a manual cryptographic hash every time a dependency changes.
The fix: Always use cargoLock.lockFile = ./Cargo.lock;.

title: Rust Packages with Cargo
text:
The boring rule

Always commit Cargo.lock to source control.
Use rustPlatform.buildRustPackage with cargoLock.lockFile.
Tests run automatically (cargo test); disable with doCheck = false; only when necessary.

title: Rust Packages with Cargo

title: Python Packages with Pip and Setuptools
text:
Python Packages with Pip and Setuptools
Python packaging traditionally relies on virtual environments and mutable PyPI downloads. The boring default is: use python3.pkgs.buildPythonApplication or buildPythonPackage with declarative dependencies, completely bypassing pip install on target systems.

title: Python Packages with Pip and Setuptools
text:
Mental model
In Nix, Python packages are derivations managed under python3.pkgs: 1. buildPythonPackage: Used for Python libraries consumed by other Python code. 2. buildPythonApplication: Used for standalone Python CLI applications. Wraps the entrypoint binary with a clean $PYTHONPATH containing all declared dependencies.
Neither uses the network at build time; all wheel or setuptools dependencies are sourced from nixpkgs.

title: Python Packages with Pip and Setuptools
Python Packages with Pip and Setuptools
text:
The trap
Running pip install inside a Nix derivation. Nix build sandboxes block network access, so pip will fail trying to connect to pypi.org.
The fix: Declare all dependencies via python3.pkgs.*. If a package is not in nixpkgs, package it using buildPythonPackage or use modern tools like poetry2nix or uv2nix.

title: Python Packages with Pip and Setuptools
text:
The boring rule

Set pyproject = true; for modern pyproject.toml packages.
Place build tools (setuptools, flit, hatchling) in build-system.
Place runtime libraries in dependencies.
Never use pip install in Nix derivations.

title: Python Packages with Pip and Setuptools
text:
Try this

For complete Python projects with a poetry.lock or uv.lock, explore poetry2nix to translate the lockfile directly into a set of Nix derivations.

title: Go Modules and Node.js Packages
text:
Go Modules and Node.js Packages
Go and Node.js are the workhorses of backend and frontend development. The boring default is: use pkgs.buildGoModule with vendorHash for Go, and pkgs.buildNpmPackage with npmDepsHash for Node.js.

title: Go Modules and Node.js Packages
text:
Mental model
Both Go and Node.js follow the standard two-step fixed-output derivation model: 1. Dependency Vendoring: Nix fetches Go modules or NPM packages using a fixed hash (vendorHash or npmDepsHash). 2. Offline Compilation: The compilation step (go build or npm run build) runs in the offline sandbox using the vendored cache.
Go / Node Codebase
       │
       ├── Fixed-Output Step (downloads go.mod / package-lock.json deps)
       └── Offline Build Step (runs go build or npm build) ──► $out/bin

title: Go Modules and Node.js Packages
Go Modules and Node.js Packages
text:
The trap
Running go get or npm install inside the build phase. Both attempt to access the network from an isolated sandbox and fail.
The fix: Vendor your dependencies into vendor/ or provide the correct vendorHash / npmDepsHash.

title: Go Modules and Node.js Packages
text:
The boring rule

Commit go.sum and package-lock.json to source control.
Set vendorHash = null; for standard-library-only Go programs.
If dependencies change, update vendorHash using lib.fakeHash during development to observe the new hash.

For Node.js projects without NPM, check out pnpm-lock.yaml support in nixpkgs.pnpm.fetchDeps.

title: Cross-Compilation for Multiple Platforms
text:
Cross-Compilation for Multiple Platforms
Cross-compiling software for different CPU architectures (such as targeting aarch64-linux for Raspberry Pi or AWS Graviton from an x86_64-linux workstation) is notoriously complex in standard Linux. The boring default is: use pkgsCross.<architecture> to switch the entire package set to a cross-compiling toolchain with zero configuration changes to your package derivations.

title: Cross-Compilation for Multiple Platforms
text:
Mental model
Nix distinguishes between: 1. Build Platform (buildPlatform): The architecture compiling the code (e.g. your x86_64-linux laptop). 2. Host Platform (hostPlatform): The architecture running the code (e.g. an aarch64-linux production server). 3. Target Platform (targetPlatform): The architecture the compiled binary produces code for (only relevant when building compilers like GCC or LLVM).
Nixpkgs provides pre-configured cross-compiling package sets under pkgs.pkgsCross: - pkgs.pkgsCross.aarch64-multiplatform - pkgs.pkgsCross.riscv64 - pkgs.pkgsCross.mingwW64 (Windows)
Because your package derivations use stdenv and avoid hardcoded host paths, swapping to pkgsCross automatically invokes the cross-compiler and cross-libraries.

title: Cross-Compilation for Multiple Platforms
Cross-Compilation for Multiple Platforms
text:
The trap
Running binaries produced by buildPhase during a cross-build test step (./desk-arm). Because the binary was compiled for ARM64, the x86_64 host processor cannot execute it natively without an emulator like QEMU.
The fix: Distinguish between nativeBuildInputs (runs on build machine) and buildInputs (runs on host machine). Disable test execution during cross-compiles with doCheck = stdenv.buildPlatform == stdenv.hostPlatform;.

title: Cross-Compilation for Multiple Platforms
text:
The boring rule

Use pkgs.pkgsCross.<target> to cross-compile any derivation.
Place tools running on the build machine in nativeBuildInputs.
Place libraries running on the target machine in buildInputs.
Guard test suites with doCheck = (stdenv.buildPlatform == stdenv.hostPlatform);.

title: Cross-Compilation for Multiple Platforms
text:
Try this

Inspect all supported cross targets in pkgs.pkgsCross by evaluating nix eval --expr 'builtins.attrNames (import <nixpkgs> {}).pkgsCross' | head -n 10.

title: The NixOS Module System Architecture
text:
The NixOS Module System Architecture
Managing operating systems traditionally means editing scattered files in /etc/, running systemctl commands, and hoping different configuration files don’t conflict. The boring default of NixOS is: the Module System — a typed, declarative framework where options define what can be configured, and configurations merge automatically into a single unified system generation.

title: The NixOS Module System Architecture
text:
Mental model
A NixOS module is a function that returns an attribute set with two primary keys: 1. options: Declares configuration settings, their types (lib.types.str, lib.types.bool), default values, and documentation. 2. config: Defines the concrete values or sets up systemd services, users, and files based on whether options are enabled.
Module A (declares services.desk.enable) ──┐
                                          ├──► Module System (merges & type-checks) ──► Final System
Module B (enables services.desk.enable) ──┘
The module system handles priority resolution (lib.mkDefault, lib.mkForce), conditional enabling (lib.mkIf), and deep merging across all imported files.

title: The NixOS Module System Architecture
The NixOS Module System Architecture
text:
The trap
Defining custom options without specifying types (type = lib.types.anything;). Without types, invalid configuration values (like passing a string where a port number is required) fail silently until runtime instead of during early evaluation.
The fix: Always declare strict types (lib.types.bool, lib.types.port, lib.types.listOf lib.types.str).

title: The NixOS Module System Architecture
text:
The boring rule

Group reusable system configuration into modules.
Guard implementation logic with config = lib.mkIf cfg.enable { ... };.
Use lib.mkDefault in shared baseline profiles so individual machines can customize them.

title: The NixOS Module System Architecture
text:
Try this

In desk_module.nix, add an option workers = lib.mkOption { type = lib.types.int; default = 4; }; and interpolate it into the script.

title: Configuring Your First NixOS Machine
text:
Configuring Your First NixOS Machine
A complete NixOS operating system is defined by a single declarative file: configuration.nix. The boring default is: split hardware detection into hardware-configuration.nix, declare system identity and boot options in configuration.nix, and activate changes with nixos-rebuild switch.

title: Configuring Your First NixOS Machine
text:
Mental model
Traditional Linux systems are configured by running commands (useradd, systemctl enable, apt install).
NixOS systems are configured by editing declarative code: 1. configuration.nix: Declares your hostname, timezone, bootloader, users, packages, and services. 2. hardware-configuration.nix: Auto-generated by nixos-generate-config, declaring file systems, swap partitions, and kernel modules specific to physical disks and CPUs. 3. nixos-rebuild switch: Compiles the entire operating system closure (kernel, initrd, systemd units, /etc, symlink trees), activates it atomically without rebooting, and creates a new bootloader entry. 4. Bootloader Rollback: If a bad configuration prevents booting, the GRUB/systemd-boot menu lists every previous generation. Selecting the previous entry boots into the exact state before the change.
configuration.nix + hardware-configuration.nix
                      │
                      ▼
            nixos-rebuild switch
                      │
                      ├── Builds new generation in /nix/store
                      ├── Updates /nix/var/nix/profiles/system
                      ├── Atomically points /run/current-system to new generation
                      └── Restarts modified systemd services

title: Configuring Your First NixOS Machine
Configuring Your First NixOS Machine
text:
The trap
Changing system.stateVersion = "24.11"; when upgrading NixOS to a newer release. stateVersion tells NixOS which backwards-compatibility defaults to use for stateful files (like database directories or user home data).
The fix: Never change stateVersion unless you have explicitly audited release upgrade notes for state migrations.

title: Configuring Your First NixOS Machine
text:
The boring rule

Keep hardware-configuration.nix separate and auto-generated; do not hand-edit hardware lines.
Use nixos-rebuild test to verify changes before committing with nixos-rebuild switch.
If an update fails, select a prior generation from the boot menu for instant recovery.

title: Configuring Your First NixOS Machine
text:
Try this

title: Service Management with systemd
text:
Service Management with systemd
On standard Linux distributions, configuring systemd services involves hand-crafting unit files in /etc/systemd/system/ and managing daemon reloads manually. The boring default of NixOS is: systemd.services.<name> — declare services as Nix attribute sets with automatic restart-on-change, dependency wiring, and sandboxing.

title: Service Management with systemd
Service Management with systemd
Service Management with systemd
text:
The trap
Writing inline shell scripts with raw executable names like curl or echo without absolute paths or package references. Systemd services in NixOS run with a minimal, sterile $PATH that does not contain ambient system packages.
The fix: Always interpolate package paths directly: ${pkgs.curl}/bin/curl.

title: Service Management with systemd
text:
The boring rule

Declare system services under systemd.services.<name>.
Use DynamicUser = true; and ProtectSystem = "strict"; for unprivileged daemons.
Use systemd timers instead of legacy cron files.
Always interpolate binary paths directly (${pkgs.app}/bin/app).

title: Service Management with systemd
text:
