title: Networking, Firewall, and Security
text:
Networking, Firewall, and Security
Network configuration and iptables rules on Linux are often managed imperatively, leaving machines vulnerable when ad-hoc rules are forgotten after a reboot. The boring default of NixOS is: declarative networking with networking.firewall enabled by default, explicitly whitelisted ports, and NetworkManager or systemd-networkd.

title: Networking, Firewall, and Security
Networking, Firewall, and Security
Networking, Firewall, and Security
text:
The trap
Disabling the firewall globally (networking.firewall.enable = false;) during development troubleshooting and forgetting to re-enable it before deploying to production.
The fix: Open specific development ports explicitly with networking.firewall.allowedTCPPorts = [ 3000 ];.

title: Networking, Firewall, and Security
text:
The boring rule

Always keep networking.firewall.enable = true;.
Use NetworkManager on workstations; use systemd-networkd on servers.
Keep secret keys (like WireGuard private keys) in external files referenced by path (privateKeyFile), never hardcoded in Nix expressions.

title: Networking, Firewall, and Security
text:
Try this

In networking_config.nix, add networking.firewall.trustedInterfaces = [ "lo" "tailscale0" ]; to trust loopback and VPN traffic while blocking public interfaces.

title: Users, Groups, and SSH Configuration
text:
Users, Groups, and SSH Configuration
User administration on mutable systems is vulnerable to orphaned accounts and forgotten SSH keys. The boring default of NixOS is: users.mutableUsers = false — define all user accounts, group memberships, and authorized SSH keys strictly in code, completely eliminating untracked accounts.

title: Users, Groups, and SSH Configuration
Users, Groups, and SSH Configuration
Users, Groups, and SSH Configuration
text:
The trap
Hardcoding plaintext passwords directly in configuration.nix (initialPassword = "secret"). Because all .nix files imported by your system configuration are copied into /nix/store, any user with shell access can read the password from /nix/store.
The fix: Use hashedPasswordFile pointing to a file with 0400 root permissions, or manage passwords via SOPS-nix.

title: Users, Groups, and SSH Configuration
text:
The boring rule

Set users.mutableUsers = false; on production servers.
Disable SSH password authentication (PasswordAuthentication = false).
Use hashedPasswordFile or SSH keys; never commit plaintext passwords.

title: Users, Groups, and SSH Configuration
text:
Try this

Generate a secure modern password hash using mkpasswd -m sha-512 and inspect the formatted output string.

title: Hardware Configuration and Drivers
text:
Hardware Configuration and Drivers
Hardware detection and proprietary drivers are a major pain point on desktop and server Linux. The boring default of NixOS is: isolate physical disk mappings into hardware-configuration.nix, use community-tested profiles from nixos-hardware, and pin graphics/CPU microcode options declaratively.

title: Hardware Configuration and Drivers
text:
Mental model
NixOS separates machine identity from machine hardware: 1. hardware-configuration.nix: Contains filesystem UUIDs, kernel boot modules, and swap devices. Generated automatically via nixos-generate-config. 2. Kernel Modules (boot.initrd.availableKernelModules): Storage drivers (nvme, ahci, virtio) needed to mount the root disk during early boot. 3. Hardware Profiles (nixos-hardware): A community collection of tested NixOS modules for specific laptops (ThinkPad, Dell XPS, Framework) and cloud instances (AWS, Hetzner, GCP).
configuration.nix (Services, Users, Network, Firewall)
       │
       ├── imports = [
       │     ./hardware-configuration.nix (Disks, UUIDs, initrd modules)
       │     inputs.nixos-hardware.nixosModules.framework-13-7040-amd
       │   ];
       ▼
Unified system generation optimized for specific physical silicon

title: Hardware Configuration and Drivers
Hardware Configuration and Drivers
text:
The trap
Referencing disk partitions by volatile device names like /dev/sda1 in fileSystems."/". If a USB drive is plugged in on reboot or BIOS disk order re-indexes, /dev/sda can become /dev/sdb, leaving the system unbootable in an emergency shell.
The fix: Always use persistent /dev/disk/by-uuid/... or /dev/disk/by-label/... paths.

title: Hardware Configuration and Drivers
text:
The boring rule

Let nixos-generate-config manage hardware-configuration.nix.
Always reference filesystems by UUID.
Always enable CPU microcode updates (hardware.cpu.intel.updateMicrocode or hardware.cpu.amd.updateMicrocode).
Use nixos-hardware modules for specific laptop and server models.

title: Hardware Configuration and Drivers
text:
Try this

Run blkid on your system to inspect the persistent UUIDs of all physical storage partitions.

title: Declarative Disk Partitioning with Disko
text:
Declarative Disk Partitioning with Disko
Traditional operating system installation guides instruct administrators to manually boot live USB media, calculate sector offsets with gdisk or fdisk, format partitions with mkfs, and type mount commands. In a declarative infrastructure stack, manual disk partitioning is an unpardonable snowflake step. The boring default is: modeling block devices, partition tables, LUKS2 encryption containers, and ZFS/Btrfs filesystems entirely in Nix using Disko, and provisioning them remotely over SSH with nixos-anywhere.

title: Declarative Disk Partitioning with Disko
text:
Mental model

Disks as pure Nix modules: Disko (github:nix-community/disko) treats physical and virtual disks as structured Nix attribute sets. You define partition types (ESP, LUKS, LVM, Btrfs, ZFS), mount points, and filesystem flags in code.
Deterministic execution phases:

Format mode (disko --mode format): Partitions the raw drive, generates cryptographic keys, and creates filesystems.
Mount mode (disko --mode mount): Mounts filesystems under /mnt in the exact required dependency sequence.

Zero-touch bootstrapping (nixos-anywhere): Run nixos-anywhere --flake .#target root@host.ip from your workstation. It connects over SSH to a standard Linux rescue environment (like Hetzner, AWS, or an installer ISO), kexecs a minimal NixOS memory system, runs Disko to format drives, copies your system closure, installs GRUB/systemd-boot, and reboots into your production NixOS machine.

title: Declarative Disk Partitioning with Disko
Declarative Disk Partitioning with Disko
text:
The trap
The trap is hardcoding unpredictable predictable network device names (/dev/sda vs. /dev/nvme0n1 vs. /dev/vda) in cloud or virtualized hardware. A change in hypervisor driver can reorder /dev/sda to /dev/vda, failing the partition run. Use disk IDs (/dev/disk/by-id/...) or parameterize the disk device attribute per host.

title: Declarative Disk Partitioning with Disko
text:
The boring rule

Declare all disk layouts exclusively with Disko modules committed to your repository.
Use nixos-anywhere for automated remote server provisioning over SSH.
Keep disk configuration files modular and imported by the host’s configuration.nix.

title: Declarative Disk Partitioning with Disko
text:
Try this

Test Disko formatting safely inside a disposable QEMU VM using nix run github:nix-community/disko -- --mode mount ./disk-config.nix.
Inspect the resulting mount table with findmnt inside the VM.

title: Ephemeral Roots and Impermanence
text:
Ephemeral Roots and Impermanence
Over months of operation, standard Linux systems accumulate stale cache files, forgotten test binaries in /usr/local/bin, untracked systemd override files in /etc, and state drift. The boring default is: erasing your root filesystem on every single boot using tmpfs as / or rolling back to a blank Btrfs/ZFS snapshot, preserving strictly declared paths under /persist with the impermanence module.

title: Ephemeral Roots and Impermanence
text:
Mental model

Root is disposable: When the machine boots, / is an in-memory tmpfs RAM filesystem (or a freshly wiped snapshot). When the system shuts down or reboots, all undeclared state in /, /etc, /var, /tmp, and /home vanishes completely.
The Nix store is safe: The Nix store (/nix) lives on its own dedicated persistent partition, untouched by root resets. All packages and configurations remain instantly cached.
Explicit state contracts: The only files that survive a reboot are those explicitly bound via bind-mounts or symlinks to /persist (such as SSH host keys, WireGuard keys, machine-id, and database files).
Instant auditability: If an attacker or errant script drops a rootkit into /etc/cron.d or /bin, a simple reboot destroys it. If something breaks after a reboot, you know instantly that a runtime state dependency was not declared.

title: Ephemeral Roots and Impermanence
Ephemeral Roots and Impermanence
text:
The trap
The catastrophic trap is forgetting to persist /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key and /etc/machine-id. If the SSH host key is erased on boot, SSH clients will reject connections with WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED!. If machine-id is erased, systemd journal logs lose historical continuity. Always persist SSH host keys and machine-id.

title: Ephemeral Roots and Impermanence
text:
The boring rule

Mount / on tmpfs or wipe a root subvolume snapshot at boot.
Store strictly declared persistent data under /persist.
Bind /etc/machine-id and SSH host keys to persistent storage before enabling ephemeral roots.

title: Ephemeral Roots and Impermanence
text:
Try this

Configure an ephemeral root NixOS VM in QEMU.
Verify that creating a file in /root or /etc disappears cleanly after reboot.

title: Home Manager and the Module System
text:
Home Manager and the Module System
Configuring tools per user without root permissions is the core role of Home Manager. The boring default is: manage user-space utilities via home.packages and service configurations via typed programs.<name> options.

title: Home Manager and the Module System
text:
Mental model
Home Manager applies the exact same NixOS module system to non-root user environments: 1. home.packages: Installs packages into your user environment (~/.nix-profile). 2. programs.<name>.enable = true;: Configures shell, editors, and CLI tools, automatically placing dotfiles into ~/.config/. 3. Standalone vs NixOS module: Can run as a standalone CLI (home-manager switch) on any Linux/macOS distro, or as a built-in submodule inside configuration.nix.

title: Home Manager and the Module System
Home Manager and the Module System
text:
The boring rule

Use Home Manager for dotfiles and user tools.
Reserve system configuration.nix for kernel, hardware, daemons, and system users.

title: Managing Dotfiles Declaratively
text:
Managing Dotfiles Declaratively
Managing dotfiles with Git bare repositories or symlink scripts (stow) leaves dead links and drift. The boring default is: use home.file."<path>".source or xdg.configFile to link configuration files directly from the immutable /nix/store.

title: Managing Dotfiles Declaratively
text:
Mental model
Home Manager manages files in $HOME: - xdg.configFile."nvim/init.lua".source = ./nvim/init.lua; - Generates a symlink ~/.config/nvim/init.lua -> /nix/store/...-init.lua. - Files in /nix/store are read-only: prevents accidental in-place mutation without committing to Git.

title: Managing Dotfiles Declaratively
Managing Dotfiles Declaratively
text:
The boring rule

Use xdg.configFile for modern XDG-compliant configuration paths.
Store configuration templates directly in Git alongside your Nix files.

title: Shell and Editor Configuration
text:
Shell and Editor Configuration
Setting up Zsh, Fish, Bash, and editors on new machines usually requires copying snippets and installing plugins by hand. The boring default is: declare shell aliases, plugins, prompts, and editor settings natively in Home Manager.

title: Shell and Editor Configuration
text:
Mental model
Home Manager provides high-level modules for major tools: - programs.zsh: Configures completions, history size, and plugins. - programs.starship: Cross-shell prompt configured declaratively. - programs.git: Declares name, email, signing keys, and global ignore lists.

title: Shell and Editor Configuration
Shell and Editor Configuration
text:
The boring rule

Configure Git, shell, and prompts through typed programs.* options.
Avoid manual plugin managers; let Nix fetch and lock shell plugins.

title: Application Settings and Preferences
text:
Application Settings and Preferences
Desktop applications and developer tools can have their settings managed alongside terminal dotfiles. The boring default is: use Home Manager application modules for VSCode, Alacritty, Kitty, and browser policies.

title: Application Settings and Preferences
text:
Mental model
Home Manager compiles application configuration settings into native format files: - programs.alacritty: Writes TOML configuration files. - programs.vscode: Manages extensions and settings.json declaratively.

title: Application Settings and Preferences
Application Settings and Preferences
text:
The boring rule

Declare terminal emulator and desktop tool preferences in Home Manager.
Ensure extensions and plugins are version-controlled via Nix.

title: Combining NixOS and Home Manager
text:
Combining NixOS and Home Manager
Managing NixOS system configurations and Home Manager user environments separately creates two different rebuild workflows. The boring default is: import Home Manager as a NixOS module inside configuration.nix so a single nixos-rebuild switch updates the OS, system services, and user dotfiles atomically.

title: Combining NixOS and Home Manager
Combining NixOS and Home Manager
Combining NixOS and Home Manager
text:
The boring rule

Integrate Home Manager into NixOS using home-manager.nixosModules.home-manager.
Set home-manager.useGlobalPkgs = true;.
Enjoy single-command atomic updates for host OS and user space simultaneously.

title: Setting Up Binary Caches
text:
Setting Up Binary Caches
Compiling software from source on every developer laptop and CI runner wastes hours of CPU time. The boring default is: a shared binary cache (Cachix, Attic, or Harmonia) that stores pre-compiled store paths cryptographically signed with public keys.

title: Setting Up Binary Caches
text:
Mental model
Nix does not compile packages if the pre-built output is already present in a trusted binary cache. 1. When Nix evaluates /nix/store/<hash>-package, it queries configured substituters. 2. If the cache possesses that hash signed with a matching public key, it downloads the pre-built .narinfo and .nar archive instead of compiling. 3. If built locally or in CI, the builder signs the artifact with a private key and uploads it to the cache.

title: Setting Up Binary Caches
Setting Up Binary Caches
text:
The boring rule

Every team should share a private or managed binary cache.
Sign all uploaded artifacts with an explicit cryptographic keypair.

title: GitHub Actions with Nix
text:
GitHub Actions with Nix
CI workflows often suffer from slow tool installations and flaky runner environments. The boring default is: use cachix/install-nix-action and cachix/cachix-action in GitHub Actions to build and test directly inside hermetic Nix sandboxes.

title: GitHub Actions with Nix
text:
Mental model
Traditional GitHub Actions workflows install tools using multiple action plugins (actions/setup-go, actions/setup-python, actions/setup-node).
With Nix: - A single action installs Nix on the runner. - The workflow runs nix build or nix flake check. - Builds and test outputs are cached to your binary cache, turning 15-minute CI pipelines into 30-second cache downloads.

title: GitHub Actions with Nix
text:
Worked examples
Save as ci.yml:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: cachix/install-nix-action@v27
        with:
          nix_path: nixpkgs=channel:nixos-24.11
      - uses: cachix/cachix-action@v15
        with:
          name: desk-cache
          authToken: ${{ secrets.CACHIX_AUTH_TOKEN }}
      - name: Check flake and build
        run: nix flake check

title: GitHub Actions with Nix
text:
The boring rule

Standardize CI on Nix to match local developer environments byte-for-byte.
Cache build outputs automatically in CI.

title: GitLab CI Integration
text:
GitLab CI Integration
Self-hosted and cloud GitLab CI runners integrate cleanly with Nix. The boring default is: use the official nixos/nix Docker image on GitLab runners, mount the Nix store cache, and execute pure evaluations.

title: GitLab CI Integration
text:
Mental model
GitLab CI jobs execute inside container images: 1. Use image nixos/nix:latest. 2. Enable experimental features (nix-command flakes). 3. Run nix build or nix develop --command.

title: GitLab CI Integration
text:
Worked examples
Save as .gitlab-ci.yml:
# .gitlab-ci.yml
image: nixos/nix:latest

variables:
  NIX_CONFIG: "experimental-features = nix-command flakes"

stages:
  - test
  - build

test-job:
  stage: test
  script:
    - nix flake check

build-job:
  stage: build
  script:
    - nix build .#default

title: GitLab CI Integration
text:
The boring rule

Use nixos/nix:latest container image in GitLab CI.
Configure experimental-features = nix-command flakes.

title: Build Caching Strategies
text:
Build Caching Strategies
In automated CI environments, uncached builds destroy developer velocity and rack up huge compute bills. The boring default is: layering Nix store substitution, GitHub Actions store caching with magic-nix-cache, and fine-grained derivation boundaries so that unchanged derivations never rebuild.

title: Build Caching Strategies
text:
Mental model
Build caching in Nix is fundamentally different from traditional file-based or Docker layer caching: 1. Derivation identity: A step only executes if its exact derivation hash (inputs, scripts, toolchain, environment variables) is missing from the local store and upstream substituters. 2. Deterministic granularity: Docker caches by whole filesystem layers; if step 3 changes, steps 4–10 bust. Nix evaluates a directed acyclic graph (DAG): changing a backend package does not bust cache for the frontend or documentation derivations. 3. Cache layers: Local runner store -> CI platform cache (GitHub Actions Cache API via magic-nix-cache) -> upstream persistent binary cache (Cachix, Attic, or S3 bucket).

title: Build Caching Strategies
Build Caching Strategies
text:
The trap
The most common trap is importing the entire repository root into the derivation source (src = ./.) when compiling sub-components. A single change to README.md or a git tag invalidates the source hash and busts the entire compilation cache. Always filter source paths using pkgs.lib.cleanSource or nix-gitignore.

title: Build Caching Strategies
text:
The boring rule

Always use magic-nix-cache for zero-configuration GitHub Actions caching.
Filter repository sources so documentation, test fixtures, and scripts do not bust build derivations.
Separate heavy dependencies from fast-changing business logic into distinct derivations.

title: Build Caching Strategies
text:
Try this

Run nix path-info -r ./result on a build artifact to observe the full tree of store paths eligible for binary caching.
In a test flake, add a clean source filter to src and verify that modifying a markdown file does not re-trigger nix build.

title: Testing in CI Pipelines
text:
Testing in CI Pipelines
Running automated tests across different environments frequently breaks due to hidden state, unpinned libraries, or missing database binaries. The boring default is: writing Nix derivations with explicit check phases or NixOS integration tests that run in disposable QEMU VMs without external infrastructure.

title: Testing in CI Pipelines
text:
Mental model

Unit tests in checkPhase: A derivation can execute tests during its build lifecycle (doCheck = true). Because the sandbox has no internet access, unit tests must be hermetic and rely solely on declared inputs.
NixOS VM integration tests: NixOS provides a Python-scripted test driver that boots full multi-node virtual machines in memory, configures network bridges, starts real systemd services, and validates end-to-end integration before deployment.
Flake checks: The checks.<system> flake output bundles all unit tests, linters, and VM tests into a single command: nix flake check.

title: Testing in CI Pipelines
Testing in CI Pipelines
text:
The trap
The trap is attempting to make live network calls during checkPhase. Since the Nix build sandbox disables network access by default, commands like npm test or go test that download dependencies or ping remote APIs will immediately fail with connection errors. All fixtures and mocks must be hermetic and bundled inside the repository or derivation inputs.

title: Testing in CI Pipelines
text:
The boring rule

Always wire test suites into derivation checkPhase or checks.<system>.
Run nix flake check as the primary validation gate in pull requests.
Rely on NixOS VM tests when you need multi-service or database integration testing.

title: Testing in CI Pipelines
text:
Try this

Add a dummy test case to your project and verify that nix flake check fails and displays the failure log when an assertion fails.
Verify that network calls inside checkPhase fail hermetically in sandbox mode.

title: Secrets Management in CI
text:
Secrets Management in CI
Nix store paths are globally readable on multi-user systems, and hardcoding secrets in Nix expressions embeds them permanently into world-readable /nix/store hashes. The boring default is: never store plaintext secrets in Nix code; inject decrypted secrets only at runtime via environment variables or ephemeral files provided by CI secret managers.

title: Secrets Management in CI
text:
Mental model

The store is public: Anything written into a .nix file, passed as a string literal, or included as a file in derivation src ends up in the world-readable Nix store.
Build time vs. Runtime: Hermetic builds should almost never require secrets. If a build requires a private git repository or private registry, pass authentication via access-tokens in nix.conf or SSH agent forwarding, not inside derivations.
Decryption at deploy time: CI runners use GitHub Secrets or Vault to access private keys (such as Age private keys for sops-nix), allowing runtime decryption on the target system.

title: Secrets Management in CI
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Providing GitHub token for private Flake inputs
Save as .github/workflows/deploy.yml:
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
name: Deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: ["main"]

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: DeterminateSystems/nix-installer-action@main
        with:
          extra-conf: |
            access-tokens = github.com=${{ secrets.GH_PAT_FOR_PRIVATE_MODULES }}
      - name: Deploy System
        run: nix run .#deploy


Case 2: Supplying Age decryption key to sops-nix in CI tests
Save as test-secrets.sh:
# test-secrets.sh
export SOPS_AGE_KEY="${{ secrets.CI_AGE_PRIVATE_KEY }}"
nix eval .#nixosConfigurations.desk-server.config.sops.secrets
Invocation and output:
bash test-secrets.sh
{
  db-password = { path = "/run/secrets/db-password"; key = "db_pass"; };
  jwt-secret = { path = "/run/secrets/jwt-secret"; key = "jwt"; };
}
The Nix expression only references the path where the secret will be mounted, leaving secret bytes completely out of the Nix store.

title: Secrets Management in CI
text:
The trap
The catastrophic trap is doing builtins.readFile ./secrets/prod.key or passing secret strings into derivation environmentVariables. Nix copies the entire contents of files read by builtins.readFile into /nix/store, broadcasting private tokens to anyone with read access to the cache or target machine.

title: Secrets Management in CI
text:
The boring rule

Never evaluate or read raw secret files with builtins.readFile in derivations.
Store secrets encrypted in git with sops-nix or agenix, decrypting only on target nodes at boot.
Pass repository access tokens exclusively through nix.conf (access-tokens).

title: Secrets Management in CI
text:
Try this

Run nix-instantiate --eval -E 'builtins.readFile ./test.txt' and inspect the generated store path to see how Nix persists files into the store.
Confirm that running nix flake check does not require live production credentials.

title: Creating Container Images with Nix (dockerTools)
text:
Creating Container Images with Nix (dockerTools)
Traditional Dockerfiles rely on non-deterministic base images (FROM debian:latest), mutate filesystem layers imperatively with apt-get, and leave behind build bloat, package caches, and CVE vulnerabilities. The boring default is: building minimal, bit-for-bit reproducible OCI container images directly with pkgs.dockerTools.buildLayeredImage without running a Docker daemon.

title: Creating Container Images with Nix (dockerTools)
text:
Mental model

Daemonless image building: Nix packages store closures directly into tarballs conforming to the OCI image specification. No dockerd, root privileges, or containers are needed to build the image.
Deterministic contents: The container image contains strictly the package binaries and their exact closure graph under /nix/store. There are no extra utilities, package managers (apt, apk), or extraneous caches unless declared.
Layer caching: dockerTools.buildLayeredImage automatically splits dependencies into distinct tarball layers based on change frequency: libc and core libraries stay in bottom layers, while your fast-changing application binary sits in the top layer.

title: Creating Container Images with Nix (dockerTools)
Creating Container Images with Nix (dockerTools)
text:
The trap
The common trap is forgetting certificates or timezone data in minimal images. Because Nix images contain only declared closures, an HTTPS request will fail with x509: certificate signed by unknown authority unless pkgs.cacert is added to contents and SSL_CERT_FILE is configured.

title: Creating Container Images with Nix (dockerTools)
text:
The boring rule

Always use pkgs.dockerTools.buildLayeredImage over buildImage for optimal layer reuse.
Include pkgs.cacert whenever the container makes outbound TLS/HTTPS network calls.
Build images in CI directly on headless runners without running a root Docker daemon.

title: Creating Container Images with Nix (dockerTools)
text:
Try this

Load the image into Docker/Podman and run it with --rm to verify that only declared binaries exist inside the container.

title: Kubernetes Manifests as Nix Modules
text:
Kubernetes Manifests as Nix Modules
Raw YAML manifests lead to severe duplication across environments (dev, staging, prod), error-prone copy-pasting, and silent syntax mistakes. The boring default is: modeling Kubernetes workloads as typed Nix attribute sets and generating clean, validated YAML manifests through functions.

title: Kubernetes Manifests as Nix Modules
text:
Mental model

Nix expressions as manifest generators: Kubernetes objects are JSON-compatible nested dictionaries. Nix natively evaluates attribute sets and converts them directly to JSON or YAML using builtins.toJSON or pkgs.formats.yaml.
Typed abstractions: Instead of copy-pasting 80 lines of Deployment and Service boilerplate, write a reusable Nix function that accepts image, port, and replicas, returning a compliant manifest.
Environment specialization: Share 95% of configuration across clusters while overriding specific values (replicas, ingress domains, resource limits) cleanly using Nix attribute set merging (//).

title: Kubernetes Manifests as Nix Modules
Kubernetes Manifests as Nix Modules
text:
The trap
The trap is generating YAML with string interpolation rather than native Nix data structures. String templates invite indentation mistakes and escaping bugs. Always build native Nix attribute sets and serialize them with builtins.toJSON (Kubernetes accepts JSON as valid YAML natively).

title: Kubernetes Manifests as Nix Modules
text:
The boring rule

Define Kubernetes resources as pure Nix attribute sets.
Generate JSON directly; kubectl parses JSON natively without needing third-party YAML converters.
Parameterize environment differences through explicit Nix function arguments.

title: Kubernetes Manifests as Nix Modules
text:
Try this

Verify the generated output with kubectl --dry-run=client -f $(nix-build manifests.nix).

title: Helm Charts Generated from Nix
text:
Helm Charts Generated from Nix
Helm charts introduce complex Go text templating, fragile whitespace semantics, and disconnected variable scopes. The boring default is: rendering Helm values and chart templates deterministically using Nix derivation pipelines or wrapping helm package workflows in reproducible sandboxes.

title: Helm Charts Generated from Nix
text:
Mental model

Predictable values: Helm uses values.yaml files to parameterize charts. Instead of maintaining sprawling, unvalidated YAML hierarchies, generate values files with Nix functions that enforce schemas and cross-reference store paths.
Chart packaging in derivations: Package custom Helm charts as Nix derivations that run helm lint and helm package in isolated sandboxes, producing cryptographically hashed .tgz chart packages.
Declarative Helmfile / Chartfile: Bundle upstream Helm charts as Nix flake inputs, ensuring third-party charts cannot change unpredictably under deployment pipelines.

title: Helm Charts Generated from Nix
Helm Charts Generated from Nix
text:
The trap
The trap is depending on remote Helm repositories that update charts in place or suffer network downtime during deployments. Always vendor chart archives or pin them with fixed-output hashes in your flake inputs.

title: Helm Charts Generated from Nix
text:
The boring rule

Validate and package charts inside hermetic Nix derivations using helm lint.
Generate complex values.yaml files from Nix attribute sets to avoid text interpolation errors.
Keep chart definitions version-pinned in the same repository as the deployment flakes.

title: GitOps with Argo CD and Flux
text:
GitOps with Argo CD and Flux
GitOps engines like Argo CD and Flux ensure clusters match git state, but letting them run arbitrary, unpinned build plugins leads to drifting environments and unreproducible deployments. The boring default is: a two-stage pipeline where Nix evaluates and renders full static manifests into a deployment branch or repo, which Argo CD or Flux syncs without needing Nix in the cluster.

title: GitOps with Argo CD and Flux
text:
Mental model

Pre-render in CI: Evaluating Nix inside a Kubernetes pod on every sync loop requires giving the cluster Nix daemon privileges, CPU, and storage. Instead, evaluate in CI and commit flat manifests to the GitOps sync branch.
Clean separation of concerns:

Development repo: Nix expressions, source code, tests, container definitions.
CI runner: builds images, evaluates manifests, pushes images to registry, updates GitOps repository.
Argo CD / Flux: Watches flat GitOps repo, syncs directly to Kubernetes API.

Instant rollbacks: Every commit in the deployment branch represents the exact state applied to the cluster, enabling instant git revert.

title: GitOps with Argo CD and Flux
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: CI workflow rendering manifests for Argo CD
Save as render-gitops.sh:
# render-gitops.sh
set -euo pipefail

echo "Evaluating Kubernetes manifests via Nix..."
nix-build manifests.nix -o rendered-manifests.json

mkdir -p gitops-repo/apps/desk-service
cp rendered-manifests.json gitops-repo/apps/desk-service/deployment.json

cd gitops-repo
git add apps/desk-service/
git commit -m "Deploy desk-service commit ${GITHUB_SHA:-manual}"
echo "Manifest ready for Argo CD sync."
Execution output:
bash render-gitops.sh
Evaluating Kubernetes manifests via Nix...
/nix/store/7wq1...-desk-deployment.json
Manifest ready for Argo CD sync.


Case 2: Argo CD Application definition
Save as argo-application.yaml:
# argo-application.yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: desk-service
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: 'https://github.com/company/gitops-deployments.git'
    targetRevision: main
    path: apps/desk-service
  destination:
    server: 'https://kubernetes.default.svc'
    namespace: desk
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true

title: GitOps with Argo CD and Flux
text:
The trap
The trap is installing Nix into the Argo CD repo-server as a custom plugin. This slows sync cycles, introduces in-cluster compilation risks, and causes synchronization timeouts when cache hits miss. Keep cluster controllers simple consumers of static files.

title: GitOps with Argo CD and Flux
text:
The boring rule

Evaluate and validate all manifests in CI before committing to GitOps repos.
Keep Argo CD / Flux configurations strictly standard and declarative.
Store rendered artifacts in dedicated deployment repositories or branches.

title: Service Mesh and Observability
text:
Service Mesh and Observability
Deploying microservice observability tooling (Prometheus, Grafana, OpenTelemetry collectors) typically involves divergent Helm charts and snowflake dashboards that fall out of sync with application code. The boring default is: declaring monitoring agents, scrape targets, and Grafana dashboard JSON models directly alongside application Nix definitions.

title: Service Mesh and Observability
text:
Mental model

Co-located service definitions: When a service is defined in Nix, its corresponding monitoring metadata (metrics port, alert thresholds, scraping interval) is declared in the same module.
Deterministic dashboards: Instead of clicking in the Grafana UI or maintaining sprawling dashboard exports, dashboard definitions are generated from structured Nix templates and provisioned automatically.
Unified telemetry: OpenTelemetry collector configuration files are generated by Nix with exact pipeline receivers, processors, and exporters.

title: Service Mesh and Observability
Service Mesh and Observability
text:
The trap
The trap is manually configuring alerts and scraping rules in third-party dashboards. When service endpoints change, manual dashboards silently break without alerting anyone. By pairing service derivations with monitoring configurations in Nix, breaking changes are caught at build and evaluation time.

title: Service Mesh and Observability
text:
The boring rule

Generate OpenTelemetry and Prometheus configurations from version-controlled Nix expressions.
Couple service definitions with their metric endpoints in the same module.
Provision Grafana dashboards via declarative JSON models committed to git.

title: Managing Terraform Providers with Nix
text:
Managing Terraform Providers with Nix
Standard Terraform setups dynamically download unpinned provider binaries from public registries during terraform init, causing unexpected breaking changes and supply-chain vulnerabilities. The boring default is: packaging Terraform and its exact provider binaries directly with Nix’s terraform.withPlugins wrapper.

title: Managing Terraform Providers with Nix
text:
Mental model

Pre-bundled plugins: Nix provides a specialized function pkgs.terraform.withPlugins that bundles the Terraform CLI and pinned provider binaries into a single unified directory.
Offline execution: When running wrapped Terraform, provider binaries already reside under /nix/store. terraform init requires zero network access to download plugins.
Reproducible team environments: Every developer and CI pipeline runs the identical provider binary down to the exact compilation flags and linked libraries.

title: Managing Terraform Providers with Nix
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Bundling Terraform with AWS and Cloudflare providers
Save as terraform-env.nix:
# terraform-env.nix
{ pkgs ? import <nixpkgs> {} }:

let
  myTerraform = pkgs.terraform.withPlugins (tp: [
    tp.aws
    tp.cloudflare
    tp.random
  ]);
in
pkgs.mkShell {
  packages = [ myTerraform ];
  shellHook = ''
    echo "Terraform environment ready with pinned providers:"
    terraform version
  '';
}
Entering the shell:
nix-shell terraform-env.nix --run "terraform version"
Terraform v1.8.4
on linux_amd64
+ provider registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws v5.49.0
+ provider registry.terraform.io/cloudflare/cloudflare v4.31.0
+ provider registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/random v3.6.1


Case 2: Running init without network access
nix-shell terraform-env.nix --run "terraform init -plugin-dir=\$NIX_TERRAFORM_PLUGIN_DIR"
Initializing the backend...
Initializing provider plugins...
- Finding hashicorp/aws versions matching "5.49.0"...
- Installing hashicorp/aws v5.49.0... (from plugin directory)
Terraform has been successfully initialized!

title: Managing Terraform Providers with Nix
text:
The trap
The trap is relying on terraform init to download arbitrary provider binaries in CI. If HashiCorp registry rates-limits or changes a provider tag, CI pipelines fail abruptly. Using withPlugins guarantees complete isolation from registry outages.

title: Managing Terraform Providers with Nix
text:
The boring rule

Always wrap Terraform with pkgs.terraform.withPlugins.
Point terraform init to the pre-populated Nix store plugin path.
Lock all provider versions explicitly in Nix expressions rather than relying on dynamic registry lookups.

title: OpenTofu Integration
text:
OpenTofu Integration
OpenTofu provides a community-driven, truly open-source alternative to Terraform without proprietary licensing restrictions. The boring default is: packaging OpenTofu with pkgs.opentofu.withPlugins to ensure fully reproducible, license-safe infrastructure automation.

title: OpenTofu Integration
text:
Mental model

Drop-in compatibility: OpenTofu maintains complete configuration and state compatibility with standard HCL syntax and provider protocols.
Identical Nix packaging pattern: Nixpkgs provides opentofu.withPlugins, following the exact same interface as terraform.withPlugins.
Open registry resolution: OpenTofu defaults to public open registries (get.opentofu.org), but when managed by Nix, providers are pulled directly from the local /nix/store.

title: OpenTofu Integration
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: OpenTofu environment with Kubernetes provider
Save as opentofu-shell.nix:
# opentofu-shell.nix
{ pkgs ? import <nixpkgs> {} }:

let
  tofu = pkgs.opentofu.withPlugins (p: [
    p.kubernetes
    p.helm
    p.null
  ]);
in
pkgs.mkShell {
  packages = [ tofu ];
  shellHook = ''
    echo "OpenTofu environment loaded."
    tofu version
  '';
}
Execution and output:
nix-shell opentofu-shell.nix --run "tofu version"
OpenTofu v1.7.1
on linux_amd64
+ provider registry.opentofu.org/hashicorp/kubernetes v2.29.0
+ provider registry.opentofu.org/hashicorp/helm v2.13.1
+ provider registry.opentofu.org/hashicorp/null v3.2.2

title: OpenTofu Integration
text:
The trap
The trap is mixing unmanaged global tofu binaries with local provider directories, which re-introduces version drift across machines. Enforce team-wide adoption via flake-based devShells.

title: OpenTofu Integration
text:
The boring rule

Standardize on pkgs.opentofu.withPlugins for open-source IaC toolchains.
Distribute the toolchain through flake.nix devShells so every engineer runs the same OpenTofu version.
Manage provider dependencies as declarative Nix inputs.

title: Ansible Provisioning with Nix
text:
Ansible Provisioning with Nix
Ansible playbooks frequently fail when Python dependencies (boto3, requests, netaddr) or Ansible collection versions differ between engineer machines and automation agents. The boring default is: packaging Ansible with its exact Python libraries and community collections in a hermetic Nix environment.

title: Ansible Provisioning with Nix
text:
Mental model

Python environment isolation: Ansible is a Python application. Nix allows wrapping pkgs.ansible with specific Python packages required by your playbooks using python3.withPackages.
Declarative collections: Install Ansible collections into a predictable directory pinned in git or store paths rather than executing imperative ansible-galaxy install commands.
Hybrid provisioning: Use Ansible for fleet orchestration (e.g. bootstrapping machines, managing legacy hosts), while deploying immutable NixOS configurations as payloads.

title: Ansible Provisioning with Nix
Ansible Provisioning with Nix
text:
The trap
The trap is running ansible-galaxy install -r requirements.yml imperatively in CI. If Ansible Galaxy is slow or down, deployment is blocked. Pin collection artifacts or bundle them directly in your repository.

title: Ansible Provisioning with Nix
text:
The boring rule

Always bundle required Python SDKs (boto3, paramiko) into the Ansible derivation.
Check playbook syntax with ansible-playbook --syntax-check in nix flake check.
Restrict Ansible to orchestration; let NixOS manage internal system state.

title: Ansible Provisioning with Nix
text:
Try this

Launch the Ansible shell and verify that python3 -c "import boto3; print(boto3.__version__)" succeeds.
Run ansible-lint as a hermetic Nix check against your playbook.

title: Cloud Provider Configuration
text:
Cloud Provider Configuration
Managing cloud CLI tools (aws-cli, az, gcloud) across multiple team members leads to mismatched API versions, conflicting credential helpers, and configuration drift. The boring default is: declarative developer shells that package the exact cloud CLIs alongside configured credentials and session wrappers.

title: Cloud Provider Configuration
text:
Mental model

Hermetic CLI bundles: Nix packages official, reproducible cloud tooling without requiring system-level installers, Homebrew, or random shell installation scripts.
Environment scoping: Provide separate shells for different cloud environments (desk-aws, desk-gcp, desk-azure) where credentials and active profiles are clearly distinguished.
No credentials in Nix store: Cloud access tokens, AWS keys, and session cookies are loaded from user home directories (~/.aws) or hardware security keys, never stored in Nix code.

title: Cloud Provider Configuration
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Multi-cloud management shell
Save as cloud-shell.nix:
# cloud-shell.nix
{ pkgs ? import <nixpkgs> {} }:

pkgs.mkShell {
  packages = [
    pkgs.awscli2
    pkgs.google-cloud-sdk
    pkgs.azure-cli
    pkgs.jq
  ];

  shellHook = ''
    echo "Cloud operations shell loaded:"
    aws --version
    az version --output json | jq -r '."azure-cli"'
  '';
}
Launching the shell:
nix-shell cloud-shell.nix --run "aws --version"
aws-cli/2.15.30 Python/3.11.8 Linux/6.6.0-generic exe/x86_64.nixos

title: Cloud Provider Configuration
text:
The trap
The trap is letting developers install cloud CLIs globally via pip install awscli or curl ... | bash. These unversioned installs create subtle behavioral discrepancies during production incidents.

title: Cloud Provider Configuration
text:
The boring rule

Keep all cloud CLIs inside reproducible Nix shells.
Never write credentials, access keys, or API tokens into .nix files.
Use session tokens and SSO wrappers (like aws sso login) within the Nix shell.

text:

title: Multi-Cloud Deployment Patterns
text:
Multi-Cloud Deployment Patterns
Organizations deploying services across multiple cloud providers (AWS, GCP, Hetzner, Bare Metal) struggle with fragmented deployment toolchains and inconsistent OS images. The boring default is: building unified NixOS machine images tailored for each target platform from a single shared base configuration.

title: Multi-Cloud Deployment Patterns
text:
Mental model

Single source of truth: A core NixOS configuration defines users, security policies, and application services once.
Target format specialization: NixOS natively supports building target-specific disk images:

AWS: AMI (amazon-image.nix)
GCP: GCE image (gce-image.nix)
Proxmox / Bare Metal: QCOW2 or Raw ISO

Identical runtime: Regardless of whether the instance boots on AWS EC2 or an on-premise hypervisor, the running userspace, configuration files, and systemd services are identical byte-for-byte.

title: Multi-Cloud Deployment Patterns
Multi-Cloud Deployment Patterns
text:
The trap
The trap is using Packer with shell provisioners to mutate golden images imperatively. Imperative golden images accumulate non-deterministic state, untracked updates, and unrepeatable patches. Nix builds images from pure specifications from scratch in minutes.

title: Multi-Cloud Deployment Patterns
text:
The boring rule

Share base system modules across all cloud and bare-metal environments.
Use native NixOS build targets (amazonImage, googleComputeImage, qemuImage) to generate cloud artifacts.
Deploy the same tested closure regardless of underlying infrastructure provider.

text:

title: Why Secrets Are Hard with Declarative Config
text:
Why Secrets Are Hard with Declarative Config
Declarative configuration tools encourage committing entire system specifications into version control. In Nix, this creates a profound security challenge: the Nix store is world-readable by design, meaning any secret placed in a derivation or .nix file is exposed to all local users and binary cache consumers.

title: Why Secrets Are Hard with Declarative Config
text:
Mental model

The Nix store design: /nix/store permissions are 0755 (or 0555 for store items). Every user and unprivileged process on the host can read every path in the store.
Build purity: Builds cannot access network endpoints or prompt users for passphrases. A derivation must receive all inputs upfront.
The separation of code and state: The Nix expression defines how secrets are fetched and where they will be linked at runtime (e.g. /run/secrets/api-token), but the secret data itself must remain encrypted at rest and decrypted only in RAM or private runtime filesystems (/run/).

title: Why Secrets Are Hard with Declarative Config
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Demonstrating store leakage (Anti-Pattern)
Consider this dangerous snippet:
# BAD: Secrets leaked to world-readable store!
pkgs.writeText "database.conf" ''
  password = "SuperSecretPassword123"
''
Evaluating and inspecting the store:
nix-build -E 'with import <nixpkgs> {}; writeText "database.conf" "password=SuperSecretPassword123"'
cat result
password=SuperSecretPassword123
Notice that result resolves to /nix/store/...-database.conf which is readable by any process on the machine.


Case 2: The boring safe pattern (Reference by path)
# GOOD: Reference runtime path only
services.postgresql = {
  enable = true;
  initialScript = "/run/secrets/postgres-init.sql";
};
The actual secret file is mounted dynamically into /run/secrets/ at boot time with 0400 permissions owned by the service user.

title: Why Secrets Are Hard with Declarative Config
text:
The trap
The trap is assuming private git repositories protect plaintext secrets. Once committed, secret strings end up in binary caches, CI build logs, developer backups, and /nix/store closures across every machine that evaluates the configuration.

title: Why Secrets Are Hard with Declarative Config
text:
The boring rule

Never place plaintext secrets, API keys, or private SSH keys into .nix files or git.
Keep the Nix store strictly public-safe: assume any file in /nix/store can be read by anyone.
Decrypt secrets at boot time into private runtime filesystems (tmpfs under /run/secrets).

text:

Verify that running nix path-info --closure on your system configuration never includes files containing plaintext secrets.

title: Using SOPS for Encrypted Configuration (sops-nix)
text:
Using SOPS for Encrypted Configuration (sops-nix)
Storing secrets outside version control leads to out-of-band communication, missing environment variables, and synchronization headaches across machines. The boring default is: encrypting secrets in-place in the git repository with Mozilla SOPS and mounting them into RAM at boot using sops-nix.

title: Using SOPS for Encrypted Configuration (sops-nix)
text:
Mental model

Encrypted in git: Secrets are stored in .yaml or .json files where only values are encrypted; keys remain visible for readability and git diffs.
Decryption at boot: sops-nix runs a systemd service during NixOS boot that reads the host’s private Age key or SSH host key, decrypts the secrets, and writes them to a secure in-memory filesystem (/run/secrets/).
No store leakage: Decrypted secret files never touch /nix/store or the persistent disk.

title: Using SOPS for Encrypted Configuration (sops-nix)
Using SOPS for Encrypted Configuration (sops-nix)
text:
The trap
The trap is specifying incorrect file permissions or owners for secrets. If owner defaults to root and your service runs under an unprivileged user (e.g. postgres or nginx), the service crashes on startup with Permission denied. Always set owner and mode explicitly.

title: Using SOPS for Encrypted Configuration (sops-nix)
text:
The boring rule

Commit encrypted .yaml secrets files to git using sops-nix.
Derive host Age keys directly from SSH host keys (/etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key) to avoid manual key distribution.
Mount secrets exclusively to memory-backed /run/secrets/.

title: HashiCorp Vault Integration
text:
HashiCorp Vault Integration
Large organizations manage credentials using enterprise secret brokers like HashiCorp Vault with dynamic secret leasing and automatic token rotation. The boring default is: provisioning Vault agents or sidecars declaratively via NixOS services to automatically renew and mount dynamic credentials into service namespaces.

title: HashiCorp Vault Integration
text:
Mental model

Centralized secrets lifecycle: Vault issues short-lived, rotatable database credentials and TLS certificates rather than static keys.
NixOS Vault Agent: NixOS configures services.vault-agent declaratively to handle AppRole authentication, secret leasing, template rendering, and automated process reload signals.
Template rendering: Vault Agent reads Vault secrets and renders them into local private paths (e.g. /run/vault/token.json) without Nix needing to know the secret values.

title: HashiCorp Vault Integration
HashiCorp Vault Integration
text:
The trap
The trap is relying on root Vault tokens or permanent credentials in local files. The entire benefit of Vault is dynamic credential rotation. Configure systemd services to listen for SIGHUP or restart when Vault Agent rewrites credential files.

title: HashiCorp Vault Integration
text:
The boring rule

Use Vault Agent for automated AppRole authentication and secret template rendering.
Render dynamic secrets to tmpfs (/run/vault/) with minimal access rights.
Wire systemd reload triggers to Vault Agent template destinations.

text:

title: Age Encryption for Simple Secrets
text:
Age Encryption for Simple Secrets
GPG is notoriously complex, brittle, and difficult to automate in automated scripts and CI pipelines. The boring default is: using age (Actually Good Encryption) and agenix for simple, lightweight, public-key secret encryption backed by modern cryptography (X25519, ChaCha20-Poly1305).

title: Age Encryption for Simple Secrets
text:
Mental model

Modern simplicity: Age has no keyrings, subkeys, web of trust, or expired signature databases. A public key is a clean 62-character string starting with age1....
SSH key compatibility: Age can encrypt files directly to existing Ed25519 SSH public keys, meaning every developer and NixOS server already has a valid Age recipient key without creating new identities.
Agenix module: agenix integrates Age encryption directly into NixOS modules, generating systemd decryption services that run before protected applications start.

title: Age Encryption for Simple Secrets
Age Encryption for Simple Secrets
text:
The trap
The trap is rekeying secrets without including all recipient public keys. When adding a new server, run agenix --rekey so the new node’s public key can decrypt existing secrets.

title: Age Encryption for Simple Secrets
text:
The boring rule

Prefer Age / Agenix over GPG for all Nix-based secret encryption.
Reuse host SSH Ed25519 keys as Age recipient keys.
Always run rekey whenever team members or machine keys are added or revoked.

title: Age Encryption for Simple Secrets
text:
Try this

Convert an SSH public key to an Age recipient with ssh-to-age < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub.
Encrypt a test message to that recipient and decrypt it with your private key.

title: Security Hardening Patterns
text:
Security Hardening Patterns
Default Linux distributions ship with open network services, permissive kernel settings, and legacy compatibility protocols that broaden attack surfaces. The boring default is: applying declarative systemd sandboxing, kernel sysctl restrictions, and immutable filesystem mount options across all NixOS hosts.

title: Security Hardening Patterns
text:
Mental model

Declarative defense-in-depth: Security is not achieved by post-install checklists or manual auditing. Every hardening directive is committed directly into the system configuration.
Systemd service sandboxing: Systemd provides powerful isolation primitives (ProtectSystem, ProtectHome, NoNewPrivileges, PrivateTmp, CapabilityBoundingSet) that can be applied to any service with single-line Nix directives.
Kernel parameter lockdown: Restrict kernel attack vectors (kernel.kptr_restrict, kernel.yama.ptrace_scope) declaratively through boot.kernel.sysctl.

title: Security Hardening Patterns
Security Hardening Patterns
text:
The trap
The trap is applying aggressive sandboxing options without testing service requirements. For example, setting MemoryDenyWriteExecute = true will crash runtimes that utilize JIT compilation (Node.js, Java, Python PyPy). Test hardened services thoroughly before deploying to production.

title: Security Hardening Patterns
text:
The boring rule

Always enable DynamicUser = true for network-facing services without fixed UID needs.
Set ProtectSystem = "strict" and NoNewPrivileges = true on all custom systemd units.
Apply standard kernel sysctl restrictions globally across all base server modules.

title: Security Hardening Patterns
text:
Try this

Run systemd-analyze security desk-api on a NixOS host to review the numeric exposure score.
Add sandboxing attributes and verify the security score improves towards 0 (safest).

title: The Internal Developer Platform Pattern
text:
The Internal Developer Platform Pattern
As engineering teams scale, standardizing developer onboarding, tooling versions, and service templates becomes a major bottleneck. The boring default is: publishing a single enterprise Flake repository that exposes standardized developer shells, CI workflows, and reusable service modules across the entire company.

title: The Internal Developer Platform Pattern
text:
Mental model

The Flake as an internal SDK: A central repository (e.g. github:company/nix-platform) exports devShells, templates, and nixosModules.
Instant developer onboarding: A new engineer clones any company project and runs nix develop or direnv allow. All compilers, linters, databases, and CLI tools match production immediately.
Painless fleet upgrades: Upgrading Go, Node, or PostgreSQL across 50 repositories is accomplished by bumping the platform flake input.

title: The Internal Developer Platform Pattern
The Internal Developer Platform Pattern
text:
The trap
The trap is allowing each development team to invent their own divergent Nix flakes and unpinned package channels. Without a shared platform standard, cross-team collaboration suffers and CI cache hit ratios drop to zero.

title: The Internal Developer Platform Pattern
text:
The boring rule

Maintain a single central platform flake for organization-wide toolchains.
Distribute standardized service templates using nix flake init -t.
Expose typed devShells (backend, frontend, data) rather than monolithic single shells.

text:

title: Monorepo Strategies with Nix
text:
Monorepo Strategies with Nix
Monorepos housing multiple applications, shared libraries, and infrastructure configurations easily devolve into slow CI pipelines and tangled dependencies. The boring default is: modeling monorepo projects as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of discrete Nix derivations where changes only rebuild affected packages.

title: Monorepo Strategies with Nix
text:
Mental model

Fine-grained derivation trees: Each library and microservice in the monorepo has its own isolated derivation.
Deterministic change detection: Because Nix derivations hash their inputs, running nix build across the entire monorepo automatically skips any service whose dependencies have not changed.
Shared local libraries: Shared utilities (packages/common-lib) are consumed as derivation inputs rather than duplicated code.

title: Monorepo Strategies with Nix
Monorepo Strategies with Nix
text:
The trap
The trap is passing the monorepo root (src = ./.;) into every sub-package. This forces every service to rebuild whenever any unrelated file in the monorepo is touched. Always isolate package roots with pkgs.lib.cleanSourceWith.

title: Monorepo Strategies with Nix
text:
The boring rule

Break down the monorepo into independent derivations with precise source boundaries.
Build aggregated targets with pkgs.linkFarm for single-command verification.
Run nix flake check to test only affected code paths.

title: Multi-Platform Development and Distribution
text:
Multi-Platform Development and Distribution
Modern engineering teams develop across diverse hardware: Linux x86_64 servers, Apple Silicon ARM64 laptops, and Linux aarch64 cloud runners. The boring default is: generating universal multi-platform Flakes using flake-utils.lib.eachDefaultSystem with remote builders for cross-architecture builds.

title: Multi-Platform Development and Distribution
text:
Mental model

Clean system abstraction: Flake outputs should support the standard architectures (x86_64-linux, aarch64-linux, aarch64-darwin, x86_64-darwin) seamlessly.
Native compilation vs. emulation: QEMU emulation is slow. Nix allows transparently delegating architecture-specific builds to remote builders (e.g. an ARM64 cloud node) via SSH.
Platform-agnostic devShells: Developers on macOS and Linux get identical CLI workflows even though the underlying compiled binaries differ.

title: Multi-Platform Development and Distribution
Multi-Platform Development and Distribution
text:
The trap
The trap is hardcoding x86_64-linux into flake outputs. This breaks evaluation for teammates on Apple Silicon (aarch64-darwin) with cryptic error messages like flake output 'packages.aarch64-darwin.default' does not exist.

title: Multi-Platform Development and Distribution
text:
The boring rule

Always wrap flake outputs in eachDefaultSystem or standard system loops.
Avoid platform-specific shell scripts in build hooks.
Configure remote builders for cross-architecture binary generation.

title: Multi-Platform Development and Distribution
text:
Try this

Run nix flake show on your repository and verify all four primary architectures are present.
Test evaluation on a different system using nix eval .#packages.aarch64-darwin.default.name.

title: Build Optimization and Performance Tuning
text:
Build Optimization and Performance Tuning
Slow Nix evaluation and unoptimized store disk usage frustrate engineering teams. The boring default is: tuning Nix daemon settings (max-jobs, cores), enabling auto-optimise-store, and keeping evaluation lazy and minimal.

title: Build Optimization and Performance Tuning
text:
Mental model

Parallel builds (max-jobs vs. cores):

max-jobs: Number of separate derivations Nix builds concurrently.
cores: Number of CPU threads passed to make -j inside a single derivation.

Store deduplication (auto-optimise-store): Nix automatically detects identical files across different store paths and replaces them with hard links, saving tens of gigabytes of disk.
Lazy evaluation: Nix only computes attribute sets that are actually demanded. Avoid doing heavy builtins.readDir operations across deep directories during top-level evaluation.

title: Build Optimization and Performance Tuning
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Recommended /etc/nix/nix.conf settings
Save as nix.conf:
# /etc/nix/nix.conf
# Build concurrency
max-jobs = auto
cores = 0

# Disk optimization
auto-optimise-store = true
min-free = 10737418240  # 10 GB
max-free = 53687091200  # 50 GB

# Network efficiency
connect-timeout = 5
substituters = https://cache.nixos.org
Checking disk savings with store optimization:
nix-store --optimise
145,210 files were linked, saving 14.32 GiB

title: Build Optimization and Performance Tuning
text:
The trap
The trap is setting cores = 1 or max-jobs = 1 on high-core build machines, leaving 32-core servers sitting idle during heavy C++/Rust compilations. Set max-jobs = auto and let Nix utilize available parallelism.

title: Build Optimization and Performance Tuning
text:
The boring rule

Enable auto-optimise-store = true on every workstation and CI runner.
Configure min-free and max-free thresholds to automate garbage collection.
Keep flake evaluation pure and fast by avoiding large source directory scans.

title: Build Optimization and Performance Tuning
text:
Try this

Run nix-store --optimise on your local system and check how many gigabytes of disk space are reclaimed.
Verify your current concurrency settings with nix show-config | grep -E "max-jobs|cores".

title: Debugging and Troubleshooting Production Issues
text:
Debugging and Troubleshooting Production Issues
When a Nix build fails or a NixOS service refuses to start, standard Linux troubleshooting techniques alone are insufficient because the filesystem is read-only and paths are hashed. The boring default is: mastering four deterministic debugging tools: nix log, nix-shell -A <pkg>, journalctl -u, and nix-diff.

title: Debugging and Troubleshooting Production Issues
text:
Mental model

Build failure logs (nix log): When a build fails, Nix saves the complete stdout/stderr of the isolated sandbox into the store. You can query any failure log directly by store path or derivation.
Interactive build debugging (nix-shell): Instead of guessing what failed in a 50-step Makefile, dropping into nix-shell loads the exact environment, unpacked source, and build flags, allowing you to run build phases step-by-step (genericBuild, phases).
Closure diffs (nix-diff): When two system generations behave differently, nix-diff compares their closures and reports the exact derivation, compiler flag, or dependency hash change that caused the divergence.

title: Debugging and Troubleshooting Production Issues
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Inspecting build logs for failed derivation
nix log .#desk-service
@nix { "action": "setPhase", "phase": "buildPhase" }
building
go: downloading github.com/lib/pq v1.10.9
# desk/service
internal/handler.go:42:12: undefined: HandleOrderV2
builder for '/nix/store/7q9m...-desk-service.drv' failed with exit code 1


Case 2: Stepping through build phases interactively
nix-shell '<nixpkgs>' -A hello
unpackPhase
cd hello-2.12.1
configurePhase
buildPhase
./src/hello
Hello, world!


Case 3: Explaining system divergence with nix-diff
nix-diff /run/current-system /nix/var/nix/profiles/system-42-link
- /nix/store/78a1...-linux-6.6.28
+ /nix/store/99b2...-linux-6.6.30
  • Version changed from 6.6.28 to 6.6.30

title: Debugging and Troubleshooting Production Issues
text:
The trap
The trap is trying to edit files directly inside /nix/store with sudo nano. Store files are intentionally read-only (0444 / 0555) to guarantee cryptographic immutability. If you bypass write protections, you corrupt the Nix database. Modify the Nix expression and re-evaluate instead.

title: Debugging and Troubleshooting Production Issues
text:
The boring rule

Always run nix log to view hermetic build logs.
Use nix-shell to reproduce build errors step-by-step in the exact derivation environment.
Use nix-diff before applying production system updates to inspect changes.

title: Debugging and Troubleshooting Production Issues
text:
Try this

Force a build error in a local package and retrieve the log using nix log ./result.drv.

title: Testing Strategies for Nix Configurations
text:
Testing Strategies for Nix Configurations
Deploying untested infrastructure configurations directly to production clusters risks downtime and boot failures. The boring default is: testing Nix expressions at three distinct levels: static syntax checks (nix-instantiate), unit evaluation tests (pkgs.runCommand), and multi-node QEMU VM tests (nixosTest).

title: Testing Strategies for Nix Configurations
text:
Mental model

Level 1: Static evaluation (nix eval / nix flake check): Catches missing attributes, syntax errors, and schema violations in milliseconds without building anything.
Level 2: Build verification: Compiles all packages and derivations in sandboxes, guaranteeing that sources build without network access.
Level 3: NixOS VM integration tests: Boots real virtual machines in QEMU, scripts multi-node interactions in Python (e.g. client sends HTTP request to server, server reads database), and asserts systemd service states.

title: Testing Strategies for Nix Configurations
Testing Strategies for Nix Configurations
text:
The trap
The trap is relying only on local manual testing. NixOS VM tests run headlessly in CI without requiring real hardware, cloud accounts, or Docker privileges.

title: Testing Strategies for Nix Configurations
text:
The boring rule

Run nix flake check in CI on every pull request.
Write multi-node NixOS VM tests for services with network dependencies.
Treat infrastructure tests as mandatory gates before production merges.

text:
Try this

Add a failing assertion to the test script and verify that nix-build exits with a non-zero code.

title: Maintenance, Upgrades, and Migration
text:
Maintenance, Upgrades, and Migration
Operating systems and software packages inevitably accumulate deprecations, security advisories, and schema upgrades. The boring default is: locking flake.lock with monthly scheduled updates, verifying upgrades in staging with nixos-rebuild dry-activate, and performing instant rollbacks if issues occur.

title: Maintenance, Upgrades, and Migration
text:
Mental model

Deterministic upgrade cadence: Flake inputs are locked in flake.lock. Upgrades do not happen spontaneously; they are triggered intentionally with nix flake update.
Atomic generation switching: Applying an upgrade creates a new system generation (e.g. Generation 43). The previous generation (42) remains fully intact on disk.
Instant zero-downtime rollback: If a new kernel or system library causes an issue, running nixos-rebuild switch --rollback or selecting Generation 42 in the bootloader instantly restores the prior working state.

title: Maintenance, Upgrades, and Migration
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Updating flake inputs and reviewing changes
nix flake update
git diff flake.lock
- "rev": "7e3b9... (nixos-24.05)"
+ "rev": "8a1c2... (nixos-24.05-updated)"


Case 2: Dry-run activation before touching running services
sudo nixos-rebuild dry-activate --flake .#desk-server
these 12 derivations will be built:
  /nix/store/...-desk-service.drv
these 4 services would be restarted:
  nginx.service
  desk-api.service
these 1 services would be stopped:
  legacy-metrics.service


Case 3: Executing instant rollback
sudo nixos-rebuild switch --rollback
switching from generation 43 to 42...
reloading systemd configuration...
restarting desk-api.service...
done.

title: Maintenance, Upgrades, and Migration
text:
The trap
The trap is running nix-collect-garbage -d immediately after a major system upgrade. The -d flag removes all older generations, destroying your rollback safety net. Keep at least the last 3 working generations before garbage collection.

title: Maintenance, Upgrades, and Migration
text:
The boring rule

Always review input updates with git diff flake.lock before merging.
Run dry-activate to verify which systemd services will restart.
Retain previous system generations until the new release is verified in production.

title: Maintenance, Upgrades, and Migration
text:
Try this

Run nixos-rebuild list-generations on a test machine to view all available boot generations.
Practice switching to a previous generation and returning to current.

title: Enterprise Operational Checklists
text:
Enterprise Operational Checklists
Maintaining mission-critical Nix and NixOS infrastructure requires discipline, standardized workflows, and proactive operations. The boring default is: adhering to codified operational checklists for repository structure, CI/CD validation, and fleet maintenance.

title: Enterprise Operational Checklists
text:
Mental model
Operational excellence in declarative infrastructure is built on predictability. When every repository follows the same layout, every CI pipeline enforces the same gates, and every server follows the same maintenance lifecycle, human error is eliminated.

title: Enterprise Operational Checklists
text:
Worked examples

The Repository Layout Checklist
Every enterprise repository must contain: 1. flake.nix: Pure inputs pinned to enterprise platform channel. 2. flake.lock: Committed to git; never .gitignored. 3. shell.nix / devShells: Complete local toolchains for developers. 4. .envrc: Containing use flake for automatic direnv activation. 5. .github/workflows/ci.yml: Enforcing nix flake check.


The Pre-Production Deployment Checklist
Before rolling out changes to production nodes:

All flake checks pass cleanly (nix flake check).
No plaintext secrets in .nix files (verified via git grep and sops).
dry-activate inspected for service restart impacts.
Staging environment verified with end-to-end integration tests.
Upstream binary cache populated with pre-built closures.
Target host has sufficient free disk space (df -h /nix/store).



The Fleet Maintenance Checklist
Executed on a regular monthly schedule:
# 1. Update channel locks
nix flake update

# 2. Build and verify system closure
nix build .#nixosConfigurations.desk-server.config.system.build.toplevel

# 3. Optimise local and remote stores
nix-store --optimise

# 4. Prune generations older than 30 days
nix-collect-garbage --delete-older-than 30d

title: Enterprise Operational Checklists
text:
The trap
The trap is treating declarative configurations as self-maintaining. Without regular garbage collection and lockfile updates, systems accumulate storage overhead and fall behind on security patches.

title: Enterprise Operational Checklists
text:
The boring rule

Commit flake.lock to git on every repository without exception.
Run automated security and flake checks on every pull request.
Schedule recurring maintenance windows for store optimization and input updates.

text:
Try this

Audit your repository against the layout checklist above.

title: Fleet Deployments with Colmena and Deploy-RS
text:
Fleet Deployments with Colmena and Deploy-RS
Iterating with nixos-rebuild --target-host one server at a time fails when managing tens or hundreds of nodes across multiple data centers. The boring default is: orchestrating parallel, tag-targeted, zero-downtime fleet deployments with Colmena, complete with automated canary node validation and rollback guarantees.

title: Fleet Deployments with Colmena and Deploy-RS
text:
Mental model

Unified fleet hive: A single Colmena hive definition (hive.nix or flake outputs) defines the configuration of all servers (gateways, application nodes, databases) in your organization.
Parallel local evaluation: Colmena evaluates all node configurations concurrently on your workstation or CI builder, builds their closures, and pushes them to target nodes over SSH in parallel.
Atomic activation with auto-rollback:

Colmena activates the new generation on designated canary nodes first.
If health checks fail or SSH connectivity drops, Colmena immediately executes --rollback across the fleet, preventing widespread outages.

title: Fleet Deployments with Colmena and Deploy-RS
Fleet Deployments with Colmena and Deploy-RS
text:
The trap
The trap is relying on target servers to evaluate and compile their own configurations. If an unprivileged edge node runs out of RAM during nix-eval, the build OOMs and leaves the node unresponsive. Always build on a dedicated CI builder or deployment machine and push pre-compiled closures.

title: Fleet Deployments with Colmena and Deploy-RS
text:
The boring rule

Define all fleet hosts inside a unified Colmena flake output.
Target subgroups using declarative tags (@gateway, @app, @database).
Use --keep-result and automated rollbacks on canary nodes during automated rollouts.

title: Fleet Deployments with Colmena and Deploy-RS
text:
Try this

Run colmena eval against a two-node hive to test configuration syntax without connecting to nodes.
Check deployment graph dependencies with colmena exec uname -a.

title: Lightweight MicroVMs with microvm.nix
text:
Lightweight MicroVMs with microvm.nix
Running full NixOS installations inside traditional hypervisors (VirtualBox, Proxmox, VMware) consumes gigabytes of RAM, requires slow guest OS installations, and isolates configurations from your host repository. The boring default is: running hypervisor-isolated NixOS guest instances as lightweight MicroVMs with microvm.nix backed by Cloud-Hypervisor or QEMU, booting in under 300 milliseconds.

title: Lightweight MicroVMs with microvm.nix
text:
Mental model

Declarative hypervisor micro-instances: microvm.nix defines a complete NixOS virtual machine inside your existing flake.
Shared host Nix store: MicroVMs share the host’s /nix/store via virtiofs read-only mounts. Guest instances consume zero additional disk space for installed packages.
Hardware-level isolation: Unlike Docker containers which share the host Linux kernel, MicroVMs run inside their own dedicated Linux kernel with independent memory spaces and network namespaces.

title: Lightweight MicroVMs with microvm.nix
Lightweight MicroVMs with microvm.nix
text:
The trap
The trap is attempting to write directly to the shared host store from within the guest. The store share must be mounted read-only (ro-store) with an overlayfs layer for ephemeral guest modifications.

title: Lightweight MicroVMs with microvm.nix
text:
The boring rule

Use microvm.nix when you need true kernel isolation without the heavyweight overhead of full hypervisor VM disks.
Share the host /nix/store using virtiofs for instantaneous guest bootstrapping.
Manage guest MicroVMs as systemd services on the host machine.
