text:
Try this

Run the MicroVM runner locally and test memory overhead with systemd-cgtop.
Exit the MicroVM and observe that no disk images or residual files remain on the host.

title: Content-Addressed Nix and NAR Internals
text:
Content-Addressed Nix and NAR Internals
In standard Nix, store paths are input-addressed: the hash in /nix/store/<hash>-pkg is derived entirely from the build recipe, dependencies, and compiler inputs. If a dependency changes a whitespace character or a non-functional comment, its output hash changes, triggering a cascade of rebuilds across the entire system. The boring default is: understanding how Content-Addressed Nix (ca-derivations) and the Nix Archive (NAR) format operate under the hood to achieve early-cutoff optimizations and cryptographic build deduplication.

title: Content-Addressed Nix and NAR Internals
text:
Mental model

Input-Addressed (Traditional):

Store hash = $ ext{Hash}( ext{derivation inputs}, ext{compiler}, ext{flags}, ext{build scripts})$.
Problem: If openssl fixes a typo in a documentation comment, its derivation hash changes. Every application depending on openssl (curl, python, nginx) must recompile, even though the resulting libssl.so binary is bit-for-bit identical!

Content-Addressed (ca-derivations):

Store hash = $ ext{Hash}( ext{actual build output files})$.
Early cutoff: When openssl compiles, Nix computes the cryptographic hash of the resulting binary. If the output hash matches the existing path, Nix halts the build cascade: curl and nginx do not rebuild!

The NAR (Nix Archive) format:

Unlike standard tarballs (which record non-deterministic file order, modification timestamps, and user IDs), a NAR serializes a directory tree into a strictly canonical, deterministic byte sequence.
Files are sorted strictly alphabetically. Timestamps are clamped to Unix epoch 1 (1970-01-01 00:00:01). Permissions are normalized to 0444 or 0555.

title: Content-Addressed Nix and NAR Internals
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Inspecting the canonical NAR serialization
Let’s inspect how Nix serializes an artifact into a byte-deterministic stream using nix-store --dump:
mkdir -p demo
echo "hello desk" > demo/file.txt
nix-store --dump demo | head -c 60
nix-archive-1(type directoryentry(name file.txtnode(type regular...
The output stream starts with the magic string nix-archive-1 and encodes files in strict canonical order with explicit string length prefixes.


Case 2: Content-addressed derivation declaration
Save as ca-package.nix:
# ca-package.nix
{ pkgs ? import <nixpkgs> {} }:

pkgs.stdenv.mkDerivation {
  pname = "desk-ca-tool";
  version = "1.0.0";
  src = ./src;

  # Enable content-addressed derivation output
  __contentAddressed = true;
  outputHashMode = "recursive";
  outputHashAlgo = "sha256";

  installPhase = ''
    mkdir -p $out/bin
    echo '#!/bin/sh' > $out/bin/desk-tool
    echo 'echo "Deterministic Output"' >> $out/bin/desk-tool
    chmod +x $out/bin/desk-tool
  '';
}
Building and inspecting hash assignment:
nix-build ca-package.nix --extra-experimental-features "ca-derivations"
/nix/store/1h3x...-desk-ca-tool-1.0.0
The store path hash reflects the cryptographic hash of $out after compilation completes, enabling automatic cache reuse across unrelated input derivation graphs.

title: Content-Addressed Nix and NAR Internals
text:
The trap
The trap is confusing content-addressed derivations with fixed-output derivations (FOD). A fixed-output derivation (used for downloading tarballs) requires the developer to specify outputHash ahead of time in the .nix file. A content-addressed derivation computes outputHash dynamically after compilation and registers the resulting path into the SQLite database.

title: Content-Addressed Nix and NAR Internals
text:
The boring rule

Learn NAR formatting rules: deterministic ordering, clamped epoch timestamps, and canonical permissions.
Leverage ca-derivations for massive CI compilation speedups where upstream patches do not alter compiled binaries.
Use nix hash path <path> to compute predictable SRI hashes for repository sources.

title: Content-Addressed Nix and NAR Internals
text:
Try this

Run nix-store --dump <store-path> | sha256sum on a local store path and compare with the narHash in nix path-info --json <store-path>.
Notice how the SHA256 matches the registered NAR hash byte-for-byte.

title: Production Architecture and Threat Model
text:
Production Architecture and Threat Model
Building isolated toy examples is straightforward; building a production-grade, highly available, self-healing multi-node infrastructure cluster that survives hardware failures, automated reboots, and zero-day patch rollouts requires disciplined systems engineering. In this capstone lab, we build an end-to-end enterprise production cluster running on bare-metal and cloud servers, fully governed by declarative NixOS modules.

title: Production Architecture and Threat Model
text:
The Production Topology
The cluster consists of four discrete functional tiers connected across an encrypted peer-to-peer WireGuard mesh overlay network (10.100.0.0/24):



Production Capstone Fleet Architecture



Tier 1: Edge Ingress Gateway (gw-01)

Public IPv4/IPv6 edge facing the public internet.
Reverse proxy using Caddy with automated ACME Let’s Encrypt TLS certificate generation.
Strict nftables firewall blocking all non-HTTPS ports.
Binds to internal WireGuard interface (10.100.0.1) to route traffic to backend workers.



Tier 2: Stateless Application Cluster (app-01, app-02)

Dual active-active application nodes executing containerless Go/Rust microservices (desk-api).
Hardened with systemd sandboxing (ProtectSystem=strict, DynamicUser=true, PrivateTmp=true).
Ephemeral root filesystem (tmpfs as /): every reboot purges all state except /persist.
Internal load balancing across nodes via Caddy health checks.



Tier 3: Stateful Database Cluster (db-01)

Production PostgreSQL 16 server with write-ahead logging (WAL) and automated local snapshots.
Storage layer managed declaratively via Disko with LUKS2 encryption and Btrfs subvolumes.
Strict host firewall allowing connections only from authorized WireGuard worker IPs (10.100.0.11, 10.100.0.12).



Tier 4: Operations, Deployment, & Telemetry (ops-01)

Central Colmena deployment hub managing fleet rollouts via cryptographic SSH keys.
Prometheus scraper gathering host metrics via node-exporter across all nodes over WireGuard.
SOPS-nix secret broker orchestrating encrypted Age secrets.

title: Production Architecture and Threat Model
text:
Threat Model and Security Invariants
Our production cluster enforces five non-negotiable security invariants:

Zero plaintext secrets on disk or in git: All database passwords, API tokens, and private WireGuard keys are encrypted with sops-nix using host-specific Age keys and decrypted exclusively into RAM (/run/secrets/).
Read-only immutable runtime: Operating system binaries, system libraries, and service configurations reside under read-only /nix/store paths (0555). No process, including root, can modify running binaries in-place.
Impermanent root filesystems: Worker nodes boot to tmpfs. If an attacker gains remote execution and drops a payload into /tmp or /etc, a simple system reboot obliterates all modifications.
Encrypted transit: All node-to-node communication traverses WireGuard peer-to-peer cryptographic tunnels. Public IP endpoints expose zero administrative or database ports.
Deterministic rollback guarantee: Every system generation is cryptographically pinned in flake.lock. If a kernel upgrade or service regression occurs, Colmena initiates an automatic fleet rollback to the prior generation in seconds.

title: Production Architecture and Threat Model
text:
Hands-on Lab Overview
In the subsequent chapters of this capstone, you will construct and deploy this entire architecture step-by-step:

Chapter 2: Define the Disko storage layout, LUKS2 disk encryption, and ephemeral tmpfs root filesystems.
Chapter 3: Build the WireGuard peer-to-peer mesh and enforce strict nftables firewall policies.
Chapter 4: Deploy the microservice stack, automated Caddy TLS reverse proxy, PostgreSQL database, and SOPS-nix secrets.
Chapter 5: Orchestrate zero-touch remote provisioning with nixos-anywhere and manage fleet upgrades with Colmena.

title: Disko Storage and Ephemeral Base System
text:
Disko Storage and Ephemeral Base System
Every node in our production fleet must deploy onto clean physical or cloud storage without manual partitioning tools. In this chapter, we create the unified Disko storage specification and configure the ephemeral root filesystem with Impermanence.

title: Disko Storage and Ephemeral Base System
text:
Mental model

Unified disk module (disk-layout.nix): Disko formats the physical NVMe or virtual disk into an EFI system partition (/boot) and a LUKS2 encrypted partition.
Btrfs subvolumes on LUKS: Inside the decrypted container, Btrfs subvolumes are created for @nix (the store), @persist (stateful data), and @swap.
RAM root (tmpfs): The root filesystem (/) is mounted in RAM with mode=755,size=2G. Unmounted state is discarded on power-down.
Impermanence persistence: System state required across reboots (SSH host keys, machine-id, WireGuard identity) is bound into /persist.

title: Disko Storage and Ephemeral Base System
Disko Storage and Ephemeral Base System
text:
The trap
The trap is failing to mark /persist as neededForBoot = true. During early boot, the initramfs must mount /persist before systemd starts generating symlinks for machine-id and SSH keys. Always ensure /persist is mounted before root pivot.

title: Disko Storage and Ephemeral Base System
text:
The boring rule

Model all partition tables and filesystems in Disko.
Keep / on tmpfs to enforce declarative purity and eliminate state rot.
Explicitly list all persistent files and directories under /persist.

title: Disko Storage and Ephemeral Base System
text:
Try this

Run nix run github:nix-community/disko -- --mode mount ./modules/disk-layout.nix in a test environment.
Confirm with mount | grep tmpfs that root is mounted on RAM.

title: Hardened Networking and WireGuard Mesh
text:
Hardened Networking and WireGuard Mesh
Exposing internal services, databases, or management endpoints to public IP addresses is an extreme security risk. The boring default is: linking all cluster nodes into a point-to-point encrypted WireGuard mesh on private subnet 10.100.0.0/24, backed by strict nftables firewall policies that drop all unsolicited public traffic.

title: Hardened Networking and WireGuard Mesh
text:
Mental model

Overlay mesh: Each node possesses a static WireGuard private key and an assigned IP (gw-01: 10.100.0.1, app-01: 10.100.0.11, app-02: 10.100.0.12, db-01: 10.100.0.21, ops-01: 10.100.0.30).
Declarative peers: Peer public keys and allowed IPs are configured directly in Nix expressions. WireGuard interfaces establish bidirectional encrypted tunnels instantly on boot.
nftables isolation: The firewall allows public access only on the gateway for ports 80/443. All other node traffic must originate from within the wg0 interface.

title: Hardened Networking and WireGuard Mesh
Hardened Networking and WireGuard Mesh
text:
The trap
The trap is generating WireGuard private keys into /nix/store. Private keys must be created on the host or provisioned via sops-nix directly to /run/secrets/wireguard/private.key.

title: Hardened Networking and WireGuard Mesh
text:
The boring rule

Bind internal services exclusively to the WireGuard mesh interface (wg0).
Restrict public ports to HTTP/HTTPS on the edge gateway and UDP 51820 on peers.
Use persistent keepalives (persistentKeepalive = 25) to maintain NAT traversal across cloud firewalls.

title: Hardened Networking and WireGuard Mesh
text:
Try this

Bring up two test nodes on WireGuard and verify connectivity with ping 10.100.0.21.
Verify with nmap that PostgreSQL port 5432 is closed on the public interface.

title: Distributed Application Stack and Secrets
text:
Distributed Application Stack and Secrets
With storage and networking established, we deploy the production workload: an edge Caddy reverse proxy with automated Let’s Encrypt TLS certificates, a containerless Go microservice with systemd sandboxing, a hardened PostgreSQL 16 database, and SOPS-nix runtime secret distribution.

title: Distributed Application Stack and Secrets
text:
Mental model

Caddy Ingress (gw-01): Terminates TLS, enforces modern ciphers (TLS 1.3), and round-robin proxies requests across backend worker nodes over the WireGuard mesh (10.100.0.11:8080, 10.100.0.12:8080).
Hardened Microservice (app-01, app-02): Runs the compiled application binary as a dynamic unprivileged user with complete systemd sandboxing.
SOPS-nix runtime decryption: Encrypted secrets in git (secrets/cluster.yaml) are decrypted into /run/secrets/ at boot time using the node’s private Age key.

title: Distributed Application Stack and Secrets
Distributed Application Stack and Secrets
text:
The trap
The trap is allowing the web service to talk to the database with unencrypted credentials in command line arguments (--password=secret). Any unprivileged user running ps aux can read arguments of other processes. Always pass credentials via EnvironmentFile mounted from /run/secrets/.

title: Distributed Application Stack and Secrets
text:
The boring rule

Terminate TLS with Caddy for zero-maintenance ACME certificate renewals.
Sandbox every microservice with DynamicUser = true and ProtectSystem = "strict".
Inject secrets exclusively via /run/secrets/ with SOPS-nix.

title: Automated Fleet Rollout and Disaster Recovery
text:
Automated Fleet Rollout and Disaster Recovery
A production architecture is only as dependable as its operational playbook. In this final chapter, we bring the entire cluster to life: orchestrating fleet-wide deployments with Colmena, executing automated canary health checks, and performing a zero-touch bare-metal disaster recovery from scratch.

title: Automated Fleet Rollout and Disaster Recovery
text:
Mental model

The Flake as the cluster source of truth: The root flake.nix declares all nodes, their disk layouts, network identities, and services.
Automated fleet rollouts: Colmena pushes new system closures across the entire fleet in parallel.
Canary deployment pipeline: Colmena updates app-01 first. If health probes on https://api.company.internal/healthz fail, the deployment immediately halts and rolls back before app-02 or the database are touched.
Zero-touch disaster recovery: If a physical server burns down, booting a replacement into rescue mode and running one nixos-anywhere command completely reconstructs the machine in under 4 minutes.

title: Automated Fleet Rollout and Disaster Recovery
Automated Fleet Rollout and Disaster Recovery
text:
The trap
The trap is not testing disaster recovery until a production incident occurs. Schedule automated recovery drills quarterly: wipe a staging server completely and run nixos-anywhere to prove your declarative configurations remain 100% self-sufficient.

title: Automated Fleet Rollout and Disaster Recovery
text:
The boring rule

Model the entire multi-node cluster inside a single Colmena flake.
Enforce canary node verification before rolling out cluster-wide updates.
Verify that every server can be rebuilt from scratch with a single nixos-anywhere command.

Review the generated closure sizes with colmena exec nix-store --gc --print-roots.

title: Glossary of Terms
text:
Glossary of Terms
A concise, definitive reference for Nix and NixOS terminology.

Derivation (.drv)
The fundamental build specification in Nix. A derivation is an immutable file in the /nix/store describing exactly which inputs, tools, environment variables, and build scripts are required to produce an output artifact.


Nix Store (/nix/store)
The cryptographic, content-addressable filesystem where all packages, configurations, and build products reside. Paths are uniquely identified by a 32-character base32 hash derived from their inputs or contents.


Closure
The complete, self-contained set of all store paths required to run an application or boot an operating system. A closure has zero implicit external dependencies.


Flake
A standardized file layout centered on flake.nix and flake.lock that provides hermetic evaluation, explicit input pinning, and standardized outputs across all Nix repositories without global state.


DevShell
A temporary, isolated shell environment created by nix develop or nix-shell containing exactly the compilers, libraries, and tools specified for a project.


Binary Cache / Substituter
An HTTP service (such as cache.nixos.org, Cachix, or Attic) serving pre-compiled store closures. When Nix requires a store path, it queries substituters before compiling from source.


Garbage Collection Root (GC Root)
A symlink outside the Nix store (such as /run/current-system or result) that protects a store path and its entire dependency closure from being deleted by nix-collect-garbage.


Home Manager
A declarative user-environment management system using Nix modules to configure user-space dotfiles, shell environments, and user applications.


Overlay
A Nix function with signature final: prev: { ... } used to modify, override, or extend packages in nixpkgs without editing upstream files.


Module System
The extensible configuration engine powering NixOS and Home Manager. Modules define typed options and assign config values that merge deterministically across multiple files.
